title: Meta TLX Brings Warp-Group GPU Control to Triton on Hopper, Blackwell, AMD
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Meta has published a detailed report on TLX (Triton Low-Level Extensions) . It is the GPU compiler extension behind Meta’s production ML kernels. Meta TLX is a Triton extension that exposes warp groups, barriers, TMA and clusters to Python kernels. It targets NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell plus AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. For kernel engineers, the message is CUDA-level control without leaving Triton. TL;DR What it is: an extension to Triton, not a new language. A Blackwell GEMM takes roughly 200 lines of Python-level Triton . Runs on: NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200, GB200), AMD MI300 and MI350-series. MIT-licensed. Performance: within -0.9% to +3.7% of cuBLAS on 6 H100 FP16 GEMM shapes ( PyTorch ). Best: a 4x speedup on an H100 linear compression kernel for ads inference ( Meta ). Worst: dense LLM-style attention forward reaches about 87% of FlashAttention-4 on B200 ( PyTorch ). Bottom line: Best: hand-tuned performance from short Triton code. Worst: all numbers are self-reported, with no independent benchmarks yet. What is TLX and what problem does it solve? Triton programs GPUs at the block level. CUDA programs them at the thread level. Modern GPUs need something in between. Hopper introduced warp specialization and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA). Blackwell added tensor memory (TMEM), cluster execution and paired-CTA execution. Meta says CUDA could express these patterns, but only with large amounts of architecture-specific code. TLX fills that gap with a model the research team calls MIMW (Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp) . The warp group becomes the basic unit of orchestration. Triton still defines what runs. TLX defines how it is orchestrated. Engineers write ordinary Triton and add TLX calls only where control matters. How does TLX work? TLX adds 5 extension areas on top of Triton: Warp-group orchestration: warp groups get roles such as producer, consumer and epilogue. Synchronization: warp groups sync through hardware mbarriers. Thread-level sync stays with the compiler. Memory orchestration: direct access to TMA, asynchronous tensor-core ops and TMEM. Cluster execution: multiple CTAs cooperate through distributed shared memory and cluster-wide barriers. Optional layouts: the compiler infers layouts. Programmers override them only for speed. The API reads like Triton. Meta’s Blackwell matmul example uses tlx.local_alloc , tlx.alloc_barr

summary.tldr:
Meta has released TLX (Triton Low-Level Extensions), an MIT-licensed extension for the Triton compiler designed to provide CUDA-level hardware control while maintaining Python-based kernel development. TLX targets NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200, GB200) architectures, as well as AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. By introducing a Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp (MIMW) programming model, TLX allows engineers to orchestrate warp groups, hardware barriers, the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), and cluster execution without the verbosity of raw CUDA, effectively bridging the gap between block-level Triton abstractions and thread-level hardware capabilities.

Technically, TLX functions as an orchestration layer where the warp group serves as the primary unit of execution. It introduces five specific extension areas: warp-group orchestration (producer/consumer/epilogue roles), hardware-level mbarriers for synchronization, direct TMA and asynchronous tensor-core operations, cluster-wide shared memory management, and manual layout overrides. Meta reports that a Blackwell GEMM can be implemented in approximately 200 lines of Python-based Triton code. Performance benchmarks on six H100 FP16 GEMM shapes show results ranging from -0.9% to +3.7% compared to cuBLAS, while specific internal use cases, such as an H100 linear compression kernel for ads inference, achieved a 4x speedup. Conversely, dense LLM-style attention forward passes on B200 hardware currently reach approximately 87% of FlashAttention-4 performance.
takeaways: **Architecture Support:** Compatible with NVIDIA Hopper (H100), Blackwell (B200, GB200), and AMD MI300/MI350-series GPUs.
**Performance Metrics:** Achieved -0.9% to +3.7% performance parity with cuBLAS on H100 FP16 GEMM shapes and a 4x speedup on specific ads inference linear compression kernels.
**Programming Model:** Implements a Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp (MIMW) model where warp groups act as the primary unit of orchestration, utilizing hardware mbarriers for synchronization.
**Key Features:** Adds five extension areas to Triton, including direct TMA access, cluster execution, and explicit warp-group role assignment (producer, consumer, epilogue).
**Caveats:** All performance data is self-reported by Meta with no independent third-party benchmarking currently available.

title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
author: Rong-Ching Chang, Hao-Chuan Wang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Rong-Ching Chang , Hao-Chuan Wang

Abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.

summary.tldr:
In a study of 168 participants, researchers Rong-Ching Chang and Hao-Chuan Wang investigated how the number of AI agents and their behavioral configuration influence human productivity and idea diversity during brainstorming sessions. The experiment compared human-human dyads against human-AI teams, testing two variables: the number of AI partners (one versus two) and the AI's behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant). Results indicate that while two-AI teams generated a higher total volume of ideas on shared boards, they caused a substantial decline in the number of human-authored ideas compared to single-AI setups.

Technical findings reveal that the effectiveness of AI formation is highly sensitive to team size. In single-AI conditions, participants paired with an 'average-calibrated' AI outperformed all other configurations. However, this performance advantage disappeared when a second AI was introduced. The study identified a negative correlation between AI posting volume and human contribution, suggesting that high-frequency AI output may crowd out human input. Conversely, social interaction from the AI was found to be a positive predictor of human idea generation. While the presence of any AI increased the global diversity of human ideas, only the addition of a second AI agent significantly improved within-session idea differentiation.
takeaways: **Study Scope:** Controlled experiment with N=168 participants comparing human-human dyads against teams with one or two AI agents.
**Productivity Trade-off:** Two-AI teams increased total board posts but caused a significant decrease in human-authored idea contributions.
**Formation Sensitivity:** The performance benefit of 'average-calibrated' AI behavior is exclusive to single-agent teams and does not scale to multi-agent environments.
**Interaction Dynamics:** AI social talk positively correlates with human idea posting, whereas high AI posting volume correlates with reduced human output.
**Diversity Metrics:** While single AI agents increase global idea diversity, a second AI agent is required to achieve significant within-session idea differentiation.

title: Coherence by Construction: Synthesizing CTI Knowledge Graphs and the Formal Limits of Coherence Validation
author: Tanzimul Alam Fahim, Mohammad Arif Hossain
contentSnippet:
Authors: Tanzimul Alam Fahim , Mohammad Arif Hossain

Abstract: Synthesizing relational training data such as knowledge graphs with a large language model typically emits structured objects one at a time, which keeps each object valid but leaves the relationships between them ungrounded. We study an alternative paradigm, generation by simulation: rather than describing a relational artifact, we simulate a process that produces it and take the artifact to be its causal record. Language-model agents propose intent and a deterministic referee resolves outcomes against an explicit world model, so a relation is emitted only when the event it represents occurs, making coherence a property of construction. We instantiate the paradigm for cyber threat intelligence knowledge graphs in the STIX 2.1 standard with three engines, among them an evolutionary engine applying language-model genetic operators to structured graph genomes, sharing a deterministic compiler that makes malformed and dangling output unrepresentable. We prove referential closure, causal grounding, and identifier stability, an ablation localizes each to the referee and world model rather than the policy, and two independent LLM judges reproduce the rubric's engine ranking. Our central result is cautionary, and we prove it: a validator reading any graph feature set a structure-matched random graph can reproduce is uninformative about coherence for a coherence-by-construction generator. Using Erdős-Rényi controls we realize the theorem four times, as structural separation, embedding transfer, inductive link prediction, and real-data augmentation each reward a triviality rather than coherence; we give the mechanism behind each and the conditions a valid benchmark must meet.

Notes: 21 pages, 5 figures. Includes supplementary material (Sections S-I through S-X)

summary.tldr:
Tanzimul Alam Fahim and Mohammad Arif Hossain introduce 'generation by simulation,' a paradigm for synthesizing Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) knowledge graphs that shifts from direct object generation to simulating causal processes. By utilizing language-model agents to propose intent and a deterministic referee to resolve outcomes against an explicit world model, the authors ensure that relations are only emitted when the underlying event occurs. This approach guarantees coherence by construction, specifically targeting the STIX 2.1 standard, and utilizes three distinct engines, including an evolutionary engine that applies genetic operators to structured graph genomes.

The paper proves that this methodology achieves referential closure, causal grounding, and identifier stability, with a deterministic compiler preventing malformed or dangling outputs. The authors provide a cautionary central result: they prove that validators relying on graph feature sets—which structure-matched random graphs can replicate—are fundamentally uninformative for coherence-by-construction generators. Through Erdős-Rényi controls, the researchers demonstrate that common evaluation metrics like embedding transfer, inductive link prediction, and real-data augmentation often reward trivial structural properties rather than actual coherence, establishing the necessary conditions for valid future benchmarking.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Generation by simulation replaces direct relational artifact description with a causal record produced by a deterministic referee and world model.
**Standard Compliance:** The framework is instantiated for CTI knowledge graphs using the STIX 2.1 standard.
**Core Proof:** The authors prove that validators based on graph feature sets are uninformative for coherence-by-construction generators because random graphs can replicate these features.
**Evaluation Failure:** Common benchmarks including structural separation, embedding transfer, and inductive link prediction are shown to reward triviality rather than coherence.
**Engine Architecture:** The system includes three engines, notably an evolutionary engine that uses LLM-based genetic operators on structured graph genomes.

title: TOUMAII: A 4.5M-Pair Tool-Calling Preference Dataset and Its Source-Agnostic Generator
author: Moritz P\"otzsch, Andrea Gentilini, Lisa Rossgoderer, Tom Osterfeld, Kesava Prasad Sanjivi Arul, Swanand Ravindra Kadhe
contentSnippet:
Authors: Moritz Pötzsch , Andrea Gentilini , Lisa Rossgoderer , Tom Osterfeld , Kesava Prasad Sanjivi Arul , Swanand Ravindra Kadhe

Abstract: To autonomously execute multi-step tasks, enterprise agents must reliably interact with tools, call APIs, or query databases, making tool-calling a fundamental capability of AI models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. In an environment where even a minor formatting error can invalidate a call and an incorrect decision can derail the interaction, direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets exactly this contrast. DPO, therefore, requires preference pairs rather than plain demonstrations. For tool-calling, such data, especially in realistic multi-turn settings, remains extremely scarce. To address this scarcity, we introduce TOUMAII, a large-scale tool-calling preference dataset containing ~4.5M validated preference pairs, derived from Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M (apache-2.0) conversations. The dataset consists of multi- and single-turn interactions and includes parallel and sequential function calls. Additionally, we release TOUMAII-Gen, a synthetic data generation pipeline that consumes tool-calling SFT datasets and generates a preference dataset with naturally occurring model-generated tool-calling failure modes. To validate the effectiveness of our DPO data, we fine-tune a 3-billion-parameter model, achieving performance parity with other high-quality tool-calling preference datasets. Furthermore, we release a second small preference dataset derived from ToolACE (apache-2.0), showcasing the source-agnostic nature of our pipeline. We release the complete code and datasets: this https URL and this https URL

Notes: Accepted to the 2nd Workshop on Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks (AABA4ET) at NeurIPS 2026. 27 pages, including 5 pages of main text, references, and appendices; 17 figures and 7 tables. Code: this https URL . Datasets: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Moritz Pötzsch et al. have introduced TOUMAII, a large-scale dataset comprising approximately 4.5 million validated preference pairs designed to improve tool-calling capabilities in enterprise AI agents through Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Unlike standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) which focuses solely on correct outputs, TOUMAII provides contrastive data—pairing correct tool calls with plausible incorrect ones—to address the high sensitivity of multi-turn agentic interactions where minor formatting errors or logic failures can cause system-wide task failure.

The dataset is derived from the Apache-2.0 licensed Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M corpus and includes both single-turn and multi-turn interactions, covering complex scenarios such as parallel and sequential function calls. Alongside the dataset, the authors released TOUMAII-Gen, a synthetic pipeline that processes existing SFT tool-calling data to automatically generate preference pairs by simulating common model failure modes. The researchers validated the pipeline's utility by fine-tuning a 3-billion-parameter model, which achieved performance parity with existing high-quality preference datasets. The project also includes a secondary dataset derived from ToolACE, demonstrating the pipeline's source-agnostic flexibility.
takeaways: **Dataset Scale:** TOUMAII contains ~4.5 million validated preference pairs for training tool-calling agents.
**Generation Pipeline:** TOUMAII-Gen is a synthetic data generation tool that creates preference pairs by identifying and simulating model-generated failure modes in SFT datasets.
**Model Validation:** A 3-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on TOUMAII achieved performance parity with existing state-of-the-art tool-calling preference datasets.
**Source Agnosticism:** The pipeline was successfully tested on both Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M and ToolACE datasets, both under Apache-2.0 licenses.
**Publication Context:** The work was accepted to the 2nd Workshop on Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks (AABA4ET) at NeurIPS 2026.

title: ChatAtom: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Molecular Dynamics Simulation and Visualization
author: Trupti Mohanty, Ming Du, Mitchell A. Wood, Brad L. Boyce, Remi Dingreville, Mathew J. Cherukara
contentSnippet:
Authors: Trupti Mohanty , Ming Du , Mitchell A. Wood , Brad L. Boyce , Remi Dingreville , Mathew J. Cherukara

Abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation resolves atomic-scale motion and predicts the structural, mechanical, and dynamic properties of materials, making it cen- tral to materials design and discovery. Yet an MD study requires an expert-driven workflow: designing the simulation, writing reliable input scripts, executing them, and analyzing the results with separate tools. Here we present ChatAtom, a multi-agent large language model system that translates a natural-language request into a complete MD workflow without the user writing input scripts or analysis code. Each agent has a defined responsibility within the workflow. An orchestrator plans the study; the LAMMPS and OVITO agents each use a generator-reviewer pair to prepare and review simulation and visualization scripts before execution; a high-performance computing agent dispatches jobs to remote resources; and an analysis agent interprets the completed run. The work- flow is accessible through a browser interface that streams thermodynamic data and rendered frames during local execution, allowing users to follow the simu- lation as it progresses. The architecture also supports new capabilities through loadable skills without modifying the agents, enabling autonomous hypothesis generation and testing. We evaluate ChatAtom through script-generation bench- marks, an end-to-end study of crack propagation, and a closed-loop campaign. By bringing script generation, execution, visualization, and analysis into one reviewed and observable pipeline, ChatAtom lowers the barrier to conducting MD studies and broadens access to advanced simulation workflows.

summary.tldr:
ChatAtom is a multi-agent LLM framework designed to automate the end-to-end molecular dynamics (MD) simulation workflow, developed by researchers Trupti Mohanty, Ming Du, Mitchell A. Wood, Brad L. Boyce, Remi Dingreville, and Mathew J. Cherukara. The system eliminates the need for manual input script generation or analysis coding by translating natural-language requests into executable workflows. It utilizes a modular architecture where specialized agents handle distinct tasks: an orchestrator for study planning, dedicated agents for LAMMPS (simulation) and OVITO (visualization) using generator-reviewer pairs to ensure script accuracy, a high-performance computing (HPC) agent for job dispatch, and an analysis agent for interpreting results.

The system features a browser-based interface that provides real-time streaming of thermodynamic data and rendered frames, allowing users to monitor simulations as they progress. ChatAtom's architecture is extensible, supporting new capabilities via loadable skills that do not require modification of the core agent codebase, facilitating autonomous hypothesis generation and testing. The authors validated the system through script-generation benchmarks, an end-to-end crack propagation study, and a closed-loop experimental campaign, demonstrating its ability to integrate simulation, visualization, and analysis into a single, observable pipeline.
takeaways: **Agent Architecture:** Employs a multi-agent system including an orchestrator, LAMMPS and OVITO agents with generator-reviewer pairs, an HPC dispatcher, and an analysis agent.
**Extensibility:** Supports new functionality through loadable skills, allowing for autonomous hypothesis testing without altering the underlying agent framework.
**User Interface:** Provides a browser-based dashboard for real-time monitoring of thermodynamic data and visualization frames during simulation execution.
**Validation Studies:** Evaluated via script-generation benchmarks, a crack propagation simulation, and a closed-loop research campaign.

title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
author: Yixuan Duan, Kexin Geng, Hanwen Xu, Wei Qiu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), a 4B parameter multimodal large language model (MLLM) designed to automate tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) analysis by reasoning jointly over paired H&E and multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) images. Unlike existing pathology MLLMs that rely solely on H&E, HERMES utilizes mIF data to provide cell-level ground truth, enabling the model to verify intermediate reasoning steps against clinical guidelines for tasks such as tissue compartment delineation and marker-positive cell counting.

HERMES employs an R1-style reinforcement learning approach with process reward supervision, ensuring that every stated quantity in its reasoning chain is checked against mIF-derived ground truth. In evaluations across four colorectal cancer TIME tasks, HERMES achieved an average accuracy of 84.5%, outperforming twelve proprietary, general, and medical MLLMs, which averaged 74.7%. The model demonstrated robust generalization, maintaining superior performance on external CODEX-imaged cohorts (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and head and neck cancer datasets (76.7% vs. 72.5%), despite these being absent from the training data. Ablation studies confirmed that the process reward is critical, as reinforcement learning without it yielded only marginal gains over supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%).
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** HERMES is a 4B parameter MLLM trained with process reward supervision to reason over paired H&E and mIF data.
**Performance Benchmark:** HERMES achieved 84.5% average accuracy on colorectal cancer TIME tasks, significantly higher than the 74.7% benchmark set by the strongest of twelve competing MLLMs.
**Generalization Capability:** The model maintained high accuracy on out-of-distribution data, including CODEX-imaged cohorts and head and neck cancer, without requiring retraining.
**Process Reward Impact:** Reinforcement learning with process rewards significantly improved accuracy and reasoning reliability compared to standard supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%).
**Verification Mechanism:** The model's reasoning is validated against 885 test questions where editing a decisive stated quantity correctly alters the final answer.

title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
author: Bao Pham
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

summary.tldr:
The research paper 'Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory' (arXiv:2611.26797v1) proposes a unified framework for understanding generative AI through the lens of Associative Memory (AM). The authors argue that generative models function by storing patterns as energy minima, where retrieval occurs via attractor dynamics. The study posits that 'spurious states'—previously considered memory failures—are actually the mechanism behind generative creativity, allowing models to blend training samples into novel outputs.

Technically, the authors demonstrate that diffusion models, including Stable Diffusion, act as AMs where training samples form distinct basins of attraction. As training data volume increases, these basins shrink, causing spurious states to emerge as attractors that represent unseen data. The researchers extend this analysis to language models, specifically uniform-state discrete diffusion models, showing that conditional likelihood maximization drives the expansion of basins around unseen examples. By utilizing conditional entropy, the authors provide a diagnostic metric to determine whether a model is currently in a state of memorization or generalization, suggesting that these two behaviors are not mutually exclusive but coexist within a single retrieval process.
takeaways: **Theoretical Framework:** Generative models are re-characterized as Associative Memories where patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics.
**Role of Spurious States:** The paper identifies spurious states—previously viewed as memory errors—as the fundamental source of generative creativity and generalization.
**Diffusion Dynamics:** In diffusion models, increasing training data causes basins of attraction around specific samples to shrink, facilitating the emergence of attractors that blend data points.
**Diagnostic Metric:** Conditional entropy is proposed as a low-cost method to measure the transition between memorization and generalization within a model's sequence generation.
**Model Scope:** The research validates this AM framework across both image-based architectures, such as Stable Diffusion, and uniform-state discrete diffusion models for language.

title: Beyond Demographic Discrimination: Benchmarking Normative-Descriptive Calibration in LLMs
author: Radhika Bhargava, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, George Mihaila, Jay Prajapati, Anwesan Pal, Yue Zhang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, where they must distinguish between normative reasoning (what should happen) and descriptive reasoning (what is likely to happen). Most fairness benchmarks evaluate demographic discrimination under a single reasoning objective, and none we know of tests whether a model treats the same item differently when asked to describe an outcome versus decide one. We introduce normative--descriptive calibration, the extent to which a model's differentiation between matched candidates depends on whether it is asked to predict or to decide, and measure it with the Normative--Descriptive Calibration Benchmark (NDCB): 697 matched-pair scenarios across six domains, each posed under both framings, and three metrics, Normative Engagement Rate (NER), Normative Leakage Rate (NLR), and Normative--Descriptive Separation (NDS). Across six LLMs, NDS separates 13 of 15 model pairs, against 7 for BBQ accuracy and none for BOLD, although these counts also reflect each benchmark's sample size. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus 4.6 separate the framings most strongly (average NDS $= +0.55$ and $+0.52$, with overlapping confidence intervals), whereas GPT-5.5's average NDS is negative ($-0.14$) under the single-pick instruction and near zero ($+0.02$) without it. In a simplified prompt template, removing single trigger words never changes the sign of a model's average NDS but can shift it by up to 0.46 and reorder models. Reversing candidate order reveals a further effect: when forced to choose between identical candidates, all six models favor whichever is listed first, and once order is averaged out their demographic-aligned lean is toward the marginalized candidate. Describing disparities and prescribing them are separable behaviors that differ across models.

summary.tldr:
Researchers introduced the Normative-Descriptive Calibration Benchmark (NDCB) to evaluate how LLMs distinguish between descriptive reasoning (predicting outcomes) and normative reasoning (prescribing outcomes). The benchmark consists of 697 matched-pair scenarios across six domains, utilizing three primary metrics: Normative Engagement Rate (NER), Normative Leakage Rate (NLR), and Normative-Descriptive Separation (NDS). The study tests whether models apply different logic when asked to predict what is likely to happen versus what should happen, addressing a gap in current fairness benchmarks that often conflate these reasoning objectives.

Testing six LLMs, the study found that NDS effectively differentiates model behaviors, separating 13 of 15 model pairs, compared to 7 for BBQ accuracy and zero for BOLD. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus 4.6 exhibited the strongest separation between framings, with average NDS scores of +0.55 and +0.52, respectively. Conversely, GPT-5.5 showed a negative NDS (-0.14) under single-pick instructions, indicating a failure to distinguish between the two reasoning modes. The research also identified a significant positional bias: all six models consistently favored the first-listed candidate in forced-choice scenarios, and once order effects were neutralized, models showed a demographic-aligned preference toward marginalized candidates.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** The NDCB comprises 697 matched-pair scenarios across six distinct domains to test normative versus descriptive reasoning.
**Model Performance:** Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus 4.6 achieved the highest NDS scores (+0.55 and +0.52), while GPT-5.5 recorded a negative NDS (-0.14) under single-pick prompts.
**Positional Bias:** All six evaluated models demonstrated a consistent preference for the first-listed candidate when forced to choose between identical options.
**Metric Sensitivity:** Removing single trigger words in prompt templates can shift a model's NDS by up to 0.46, potentially reordering model rankings.
**Comparative Efficacy:** The NDS metric successfully separated 13 of 15 model pairs, outperforming the BBQ accuracy benchmark (7 of 15) and BOLD (0 of 15).

title: Towards Robust Partial-Edit Deepfake Localization: An edit and Generator Conditioned Analysis
author: Aishwarya Fursule, Vamshi Nallaguntla, Yuan Tseng, David Harwath, Anderson Avila, Shruti Kshirsagar
contentSnippet:
Authors: Aishwarya Fursule , Vamshi Nallaguntla , Yuan Tseng , David Harwath , Anderson Avila , Shruti Kshirsagar

Abstract: Partial-edit deepfake localization aims to identify manipulated regions within otherwise authentic speech. Recent systems report strong overall results, but aggregate scores do not reveal whether this performance holds across different editing conditions. In this work, we present an edit- and generator-conditioned analysis of Segment-Aware Localization (SAL) using WavLM-Large and XLS-R representations on the VoiceCraft and SSR-Speech subsets of PartialEdit. We categorize edits along three transcript-derived axes, namely content, meaning change, and editing operation, and evaluate each generator separately. While both representations achieve strong overall performance, localization is noticeably weaker on SSR-Speech. From our experiments, we found that the deletion is the hardest operation, and deletions produced by SSR-Speech are the most challenging condition for both representations. In contrast, edit content, meaning change, and sentence novelty have smaller effects. These findings show that a single aggregate score can mask important weaknesses, and that partial-edit localization should be evaluated separately across generators and edit types.

Notes: Submitted to ICASSP 2027 Workshop

summary.tldr:
Researchers Aishwarya Fursule, Vamshi Nallaguntla, Yuan Tseng, David Harwath, Anderson Avila, and Shruti Kshirsagar presented a granular analysis of Segment-Aware Localization (SAL) for partial-edit deepfake detection, submitted to the ICASSP 2027 Workshop. The study evaluates the performance of WavLM-Large and XLS-R representations on the VoiceCraft and SSR-Speech subsets of the PartialEdit dataset, moving beyond aggregate metrics to assess how specific editing conditions impact localization accuracy.

The study categorizes edits across three axes: content, meaning change, and editing operation. Experimental results indicate that while both WavLM-Large and XLS-R maintain strong overall performance, localization efficacy drops significantly on the SSR-Speech subset compared to VoiceCraft. The researchers identified 'deletion' as the most difficult editing operation to localize, with deletions generated by SSR-Speech proving to be the most challenging condition for both models. Conversely, factors such as edit content, meaning change, and sentence novelty demonstrated minimal impact on localization performance, suggesting that aggregate scoring masks critical model vulnerabilities.
takeaways: **Model Architectures:** The study evaluates WavLM-Large and XLS-R representations for the task of segment-aware localization.
**Dataset Subsets:** Performance was benchmarked specifically against the VoiceCraft and SSR-Speech subsets of the PartialEdit dataset.
**Hardest Operation:** Deletion was identified as the most difficult editing operation to localize across both tested representations.
**Performance Variance:** Localization performance is noticeably weaker on the SSR-Speech subset compared to VoiceCraft, highlighting generator-specific vulnerabilities.
**Metric Critique:** The authors argue that aggregate performance scores are insufficient and that evaluation must be segmented by generator type and edit operation to reveal model weaknesses.

title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
author: Wei Jiang, Ziran Liu, Wei Wang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Wei Jiang , Ziran Liu , Wei Wang

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.

Notes: 16 pages, 9 tables, 1 figure

summary.tldr:
Researchers Wei Jiang, Ziran Liu, and Wei Wang have introduced BudgetPV, an agentic framework designed to optimize computational expenditure in theorem proving by dynamically allocating subgoals to a heterogeneous pool of LLM solvers. The system addresses the inefficiency of uniform solver application by utilizing a cross-solver predictor that determines the optimal model for each subgoal based on its difficulty and the available budget. The framework operates in two distinct stages: an initial assignment phase for untried subgoals and a subsequent revision phase that reallocates computation to previously attempted subgoals based on verification feedback.

The methodology employs a dual-objective training strategy for the predictor: class-weighted cross-entropy to ensure adequate assignment to high-capability, low-frequency solvers during the initial stage, and plain cross-entropy to calibrate probabilities for later-stage resource allocation. BudgetPV was evaluated across four benchmarks—Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench—using three solver configurations that scale from a single high-cost model to a tiered system incorporating medium and low-cost solvers. Experimental results demonstrate that BudgetPV achieves equivalent proof success rates while significantly reducing total LLM generation computation compared to uniform allocation strategies, with efficiency gains scaling as more cost-effective solvers are integrated into the pipeline.
takeaways: **System Architecture:** BudgetPV utilizes a cross-solver predictor that dynamically manages computation allocation across heterogeneous LLM solvers based on subgoal difficulty.
**Training Objectives:** The predictor uses class-weighted cross-entropy for initial solver assignment and plain cross-entropy for calibrated probability estimation during later-stage re-allocation.
**Benchmark Suite:** Performance was validated on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three tiered solver settings ranging from single-model to multi-cost configurations.
**Efficiency Gains:** The framework consistently requires less total LLM generation computation than uniform allocation methods to achieve the same number of solved subgoals.

title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
author: Congyuan Yu, Runping Tian
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced AstronautBench, a new evaluation framework designed to measure LLM agent self-improvement across episodes without updating model weights. Built within the game Outer Wilds—a title characterized by 22-minute loops where world state resets but knowledge persists—the benchmark assesses agents through three distinct lenses: world-knowledge QA, the validity of evidence cited from the agent's own recorded gameplay, and physical progress within the game environment. The benchmark includes 164 specific world-knowledge questions and utilizes dual LLM judges from different model families to verify the accuracy and evidentiary support of agent responses.

Initial testing with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners revealed that these three performance metrics often diverge, indicating that traditional task-progress benchmarks provide an incomplete picture of agent learning. For the GPT-6.1 Sol agent, correct answers increased from 14.6% to 26.8% over eight episodes; however, by the final episode, only 59% to 68% of these answers were backed by the agent's cited evidence. Furthermore, the agent ceased discovering new 'rumor facts' after episode 3, despite continued growth in physical exploration and memory, with over half of the post-episode 3 correct answers relying solely on evidence gathered in earlier loops.
takeaways: **Benchmark Architecture:** AstronautBench evaluates agents across three views: world-knowledge QA, evidentiary support from recorded frames/positions, and physical progress in the Outer Wilds game environment.
**GPT-6.1 Sol Performance:** The agent improved its QA accuracy from 14.6% to 26.8% over eight episodes, yet evidentiary support for these answers remained low, peaking at 68% by episode 8.
**Stagnation Metrics:** The GPT-6.1 Sol agent stopped revealing new rumor facts after episode 3, despite continued expansion in the number of locations visited and memory accumulation.

**Evaluation Methodology:** The benchmark utilizes 164 world-knowledge questions and employs two LLM judges from different model families to verify the consistency between agent answers and cited evidence.

title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting
author: Yang Liu, Shengbo Tong, Xiyuan Chen, Shiwei Hou, Sen Yuan, Hao Wang, Yanfeng Li, Hongwen Li, Yiming Zhu, Zhuolun He, Wenjian Yu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yang Liu , Shengbo Tong , Xiyuan Chen , Shiwei Hou , Sen Yuan , Hao Wang , Yanfeng Li , Hongwen Li , Yiming Zhu , Zhuolun He , Wenjian Yu

Abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).

Notes: Submitted to DATE 2027. 7 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables

summary.tldr:
Researchers Yang Liu, Shengbo Tong, Xiyuan Chen, Shiwei Hou, Sen Yuan, Hao Wang, Yanfeng Li, Hongwen Li, Yiming Zhu, Zhuolun He, and Wenjian Yu submitted a paper to DATE 2027 titled "Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting," introducing ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution). Designed to overcome the bottlenecks of sparsely documented proprietary APIs and cryptic execution failures in electronic design automation (EDA) scripting, ZhuLong-SE functions as an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces.

The framework extends the original ZhuLong task-level harness by incorporating API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, combined with governed cross-task self-evolution. Rather than operating purely per-task, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval.

Evaluated on the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness with self-evolution disabled achieves a 92.4% pass@1 rate, outperforming the base ZhuLong across all five tested LLM backbones. On a more challenging instance-disjoint test set, enabling self-evolution from a bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points, reaching 80.0% pass@1 compared to the baseline's 77.5%.

**Benchmark Performance:** Evaluated on the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, achieving 92.4% pass@1 with self-evolution disabled.
**Memory Architecture:** Utilizes a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval.
**Instance-Disjoint Comparison:** On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from a bare configuration achieves 80.0% pass@1, beating the human-crafted-experience baseline of 77.5%.

title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
author: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Kamesh Krishnamurthy
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.

title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
author: Ashley Zhang, Narmeen Fatimah Oozeer, Aleksandr Zverianskii, Daniel Ng, Tasana Pejovic, Ant\'ia Garc\'ia, Jacob Clyne, Ravpreet Setia, Akshay Utture, Etan Jacob Ginsberg, Shriyash Kaustubh Upadhyay, Fazl Barez
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.

title: Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents
author: Deepak Waghmare, Shaad Sufi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic suppliers: 2,400 fault episodes across four policies, 60 process-termination/restart episodes, 19,000 timed calls across 19 configurations, five targeted mutations over 43 fixtures, and 160 substitution records. No language model or autonomous agent is evaluated. OPCP and a conservative composition agree on all measured fault outcomes. Both recover after definite refusal without cross-supplier duplication; retry-all duplicates effects in every tested lost-reply-after-commit case. Persistent runtime state prevents cross-supplier replay in the restart experiments, while same-supplier duplicate prevention also requires supplier idempotency. At 128 suppliers, best-score routing has a median latency of 1.411 ms versus 0.261 ms for pinned routing. All five selected mutations are detected, and record enumeration exposes acceptance of an empty regression set. These results characterize an execution mechanism relevant to agent governance, including its costs and assumption boundaries. They do not establish improved agent task success, prompt-injection resistance, or real-vendor model portability.

title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
author: Soheil Zibakhsh, Pedram Aghazadeh, Farinaz Koushanfar
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.

title: MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs
author: Vinnam Kim, Seong Hoon Seo, Junhan Kim, Jaeseong You, An Chen
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold with llama.cpp Hexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy than llama.cpp's sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.

title: From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness
author: Ji Sub Choi, Whan Choi, Seo Yeon Gu, Suhyun Kim, Inyong Yun
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. We therefore evaluate examination requirement by requirement and make each requirement executable. A language model converts the bill of lading (BL) and commercial invoice (IV) requirements of a credit into atomic conditions and logical structures, and a deterministic verifier retrieves the named evidence and computes each outcome, so every check can be compared with a gold encoding and traced to logged evidence. Because LC records are confidential, our on-premises 9B parser is fine-tuned only on synthetic pairs built from templates and human-reviewed public document values. On 345 real LC cases, final-decision accuracy proves misleading: a constant PASS rule has the highest raw accuracy while examining nothing. Although it never sees a real record during training, the fine-tuned parser detects 93% of the atomic requirements its ontology covers and reconstructs 86% of the covered requirements exactly. It verifies 82% of the evaluable requirements correctly, against 54% for a tool-using agent, and leads the agent on both satisfied requirements and discrepancies. It also completely examines 1.8 times as many cases as few-shot prompting of the same model, while direct prediction and the agent complete none. Executing the gold encodings with the same verifier shows that some of the remaining errors, missed discrepancies included, come from the operators and normalization, which a better parser alone cannot fix. Every rejection comes with a trace of the units and evidence behind it, which suits examiner-in-the-loop review.

title: Reward Integrity in Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for LLM Guardrail Red-Teaming
author: Chengming Liu, Leon Viti, Hongxu Chen, Erdem Kemik, Mary-Anne Williams, Ruth Oliver
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study reward fidelity in an adversarial reinforcement-learning loop for red-teaming financial-services language-model guardrails. Apparent wins can arise when an attack omits prescribed personally identifiable information (PII), or when a reward judge credits a response that did not break the targeted policy. On attacker-generated and public benchmark examples, TypeSafe Jev checks whether the prescribed PII is present. For outcome scoring, we compare the decision models TypeSafe Jev, Laya (pretrained and post-trained), and pretrained CLM-8B with logged Opus 4.8 judgements from a replay corpus. Post-training markedly improves Laya's agreement with the judge. A separate author-reviewed off-target set establishes that Opus can award false wins. The findings motivate specialised decision-model judges for checking prescribed PII in attack inputs and scoring target responses against the intended policy.

title: Scalable Evaluation of Medical AI using Evidence-based Practice Recommendations
author: Teya Bergamaschi, Bijal Rajput, Akshay Goel, Matthew Thompson, Jacqueline Shreibati, Dave Steiner, Ashley Carrick, Mahvish Nagda, Dale R. Webster, Avinatan Hassidim, Katherine Chou, Yossi Matias, Po-Hsuan Cameron Chen, Christina Chen, Mike Schaekermann, Yun Liu, Anil Palepu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.27007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rigorously evaluating medical artificial intelligence (AI) requires testing open-ended clinical management across diverse presentations and stages of care. However, existing benchmarks rely on manual expert authoring, limiting coverage across conditions, conditional care pathways, and evolving guidelines. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts and verifies structured clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations to generate scenarios spanning the care continuum, including nuanced presentations and practice variations across regions and guideline editions. Applied to 436 BMJ Best Practice clinical monographs (354 US, 82 International), this yields 3,200 scenarios spanning differential diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus targeted suites for regional specificity (731 US/International pairs) and temporal freshness (630 scenarios). To grade responses, we develop a clinician-calibrated autorater that scores management plans on a 4-point rubric stratifying deviations by clinical severity. Across Gemini models, scaling improves adherence, while web search (+0.8 percentage points [pp] on average) and multi-sample synthesis (+2.2 pp) combine additively (+2.8 pp). In context, full monographs consistently trail condensed excerpts. On targeted suites, web search narrows international performance gaps (+4.2 pp) and improves adherence to newly updated guidance (+4.6 pp). In a study with Primary Care Physicians (n = 9) across 200 scenarios, AI assistance raises adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%, driven largely by fewer clinical omissions. Overall, our results demonstrate a scalable evaluation setup using an evidence-based corpus originally written to guide human clinical decision-making, and demonstrate its viability to assess medical AI and its assistance on clinician decision-making.

title: SkillPrivus: Uncovering PRIVacy of USe Harms in Agentic Skills
author: Mariana Fernandez-Espinosa, Ivoline Ngong, Keerthiram Murugesan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users' files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. We study these potential privacy-of-use harms through SkillPrivus, a static audit framework that analyzes skills before installation without executing them. SkillPrivus extracts data operations from code and natural-language instructions, grounds them in source evidence, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess their appropriateness. Applied to 726 real skills from public marketplaces, 563 of which handle personal data, SkillPrivus flags at least one potential violation in 307 of these skills (54.5%), and its judgments agree with three blind human annotators on 83.2% of resolvable moves. The flagged behaviors include sensitive inferences, information use beyond the stated task, and disclosures to unexpected recipients, suggesting that privacy harms can arise from ordinary skill functionality.

title: Reinforcement Learning Unlearns Corrupted SFT Reasoning
author: Anika Misra, Shreyas Vinod, Huteng Dai
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that reinforcement learning (RL) in reasoning tasks can succeed even when the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data is severely corrupted. In a mathematical reasoning dataset (GSM8K), we systematically corrupt training trajectories across 361 configurations by injecting realistic error types, varying error locations, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratios up to 100%. While aggregated SFT-only performance steadily deteriorates under corruption (dropping from 43.61% to 13.80%), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training consistently restores model accuracy back to gold-baseline levels (approximately 60%). Crucially, initializing RL with as few as N = 8 minimal, incorrect, three-line "form-only" traces boosts post-RL performance to 69.30%, outperforming standard gold SFT initialization (60.71%) and GRPO without SFT (35.00%). Further, we show that SFT accuracy is largely uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r approximately 0), demonstrating a fundamental asymmetry in post-training: SFT primarily establishes structural layout (form), while RL independently discovers functional reasoning (function).

title: Know Your Context Bank: Repairing Inconsistency and Measuring Generalization in Context-Aware Text-to-SQL
author: Hailong Li, Mohammadreza Pourreza, Tal Neiman, Reza Sherkat, Per Jacobsson, Yannis Papakonstantinou
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on context banks: curated collections of example queries, metric definitions, and domain knowledge that tell a model how an organization writes its queries. In the enterprise, a bank grows over years as many analysts add entries, checked one at a time for correctness (does the SQL answer its own question?) and rarely for consistency with one another. Yet correctness is often loosely defined: a question seldom fixes how an entity is counted or which table defines it, so two entries can each pass review yet resolve the same decision in opposite ways. We call this condition context bank rot. A second question follows: does a system that uses a bank generalize from it, or only reproduce it? Existing benchmarks cannot tell, as they do not control how far a test question sits from the context. We answer both questions by comparing queries decision by decision, with a fast scorer distilled from human-calibrated LLM judges. Turned inward, the comparison diagnoses and repairs a bank. Fine-tuning on a cleaned BIRD-train bank beats a same-size random subset at every epoch (+2.6 points on average), and 92.4% of our removals had their SQL corrected by an independent expert audit, against 45.6% of audited entries. In-context examples that follow one convention beat those following the opposite one by 13.3 points, while a mix is barely better than none. Turned outward, the comparison generates test questions at a controlled distance from a bank, a pipeline we call CAT (Context-Aware Testing). On CAT-BIRD, for retrieval and fine-tuning alike, the benefit of a bank falls step by step with distance and is largely gone once about three quarters of a question's logic is new, and on CAT-Spider the benefit of retrieval likewise shrinks with distance.

title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
author: Mohammed El Amine Mokhtari, Matei Mancas, Virginie Vandenbulcke
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.

title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
author: Ziqing Wang, Hamid Palangi, Lili Zhao, Kaize Ding
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
author: Kaustubh Ponkshe, Gyung Hyun Je, Stefan Taga, Colin Raffel, Martin Jaggi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

title: Neural Geometry as a Learning Signal
author: Eric Todd, Tal Haklay, Nikhil Prakash, Matthew Finlayson, Michael Hanna, Fenil R. Doshi, Daniel Wurgaft, Thomas McGrath, Owen Lewis, David Bau, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Matthew Kowal, Thomas Fel, Atticus Geiger
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate whether the geometric structure of neural representations can provide a sufficient learning signal for improving model behavior without any supervision on model outputs. First, we fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B to answer questions such as "What month is four months after June?" by supervising internal representations of the input month (June = 6) and offset (4), which are encoded with Fourier harmonics. Second, we fine-tune the model to predict line breaks in text wrapped to a fixed width by supervising an internal representation of the number of characters since the preceding newline, which is represented by a low-dimensional helical structure. In both tasks, we supervise a low-dimensional subspace of the residual stream using an idealized target structure, and find that internal geometric supervision achieves similar performance to standard fine-tuning (despite no supervision on outputs). Moreover, we find that simply patching in an ideal geometry is not sufficient to recover fine-tuning performance, and thus demonstrate geometric supervision provides beneficial effects beyond the representations it targets. Together, these findings show how mechanistic understanding of neural geometry can be leveraged to shape the behavior of neural networks.

title: Rethinking Full-Weight LoRA with Domain and Task Adapter Scaling for Question Answering over Portuguese Well Drilling Reports
author: Luan B. Guerra, Diogo M. Paes, Marcelo N. Grimberg, Arnaldo C. Junior, Wallace Casaca, Lucas C. Ribas
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains remains challenging, particularly for technical documents such as Portuguese well drilling reports, where annotated data are scarce and domain adaptation may compromise instruction-following capabilities. Although Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for parameter-efficient adaptation, its scaling after training remains insufficiently explored. This study investigates the impact of LoRA adapter scaling on question answering over Portuguese drilling reports using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. Domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) is performed either directly on instruction-tuned models or on their base counterparts, with subsequent adapter transfer, while task-specific adapters are trained on WellQuest, an open-source question-answering dataset derived from Portuguese drilling reports. The two adapters are also combined using complementary weights. Scaling factors ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 are evaluated across multiple training checkpoints using BERTScore. Results show that fractional scaling consistently improves DAPT performance over full-weight application, increasing F1 from 68.8\% to 71.9\% for Qwen2.5-7B and from 63.2\% to 68.5\% for Llama-3.1-8B. QA adapters perform best at high but fractional weights, while base-to-instruct transfer yields better results than direct DAPT on instruct-tuned models. Adapter merging provides a modest improvement for Llama-3.1-8B. Overall, these findings demonstrate that post-training adapter scaling can improve domain adaptation without additional data or training.

title: Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models
author: Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Dennis Wei, Rahul Nair
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets

title: Cross-Linguistic Distinctive-Feature Constraints on Segmental Triphones: Evidence for Contrastive Dispersion
author: Leonardo Ara\'ujo
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.26837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural speech reflects articulatory and perceptual constraints, yet how these pressures shape consecutive segment transitions across languages remains underexplored. We analyze adjacent distinctive-feature distances in token-weighted segmental triphones across 17 Universal Dependencies corpora spanning nine language families, transcribed into IPA and mapped to 24 PanPhon features using Hamming and cosine metrics. Natural sequences exhibit an intermediate-distance mode (8-10 features under Hamming, except Vietnamese; 0.28-0.38 under cosine). Against an unrestricted within-word shuffled baseline, natural words reject the inventory-only null (W = 0, p < 10-4), showing higher expected distance, narrower dispersion, and lower joint triphone entropy in all 17 languages. Under a stricter within-word consonant-vowel template baseline, expected distance and dispersion are no longer separated, whereas joint entropy remains lower in 16 languages (p = 1.07x10-4). Entropy decomposition reveals higher mutual information between incoming and outgoing transitions in all 17 languages and all nine families (W = 0, p < 10-4), demonstrating sequential coupling beyond syllable-template alternation. Word-level mean-SD correlations and directional asymmetries do not replicate cross-linguistically.
