title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
author: Chi Yan, Guoyang Zhao, Wentao Yuan, Yixiao Ge
contentSnippet: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy (δ_1) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

summary.tldr:
StereoVLM is a geometry-aware binocular vision-language model designed to address the limitations of standard VLMs in metric 3D spatial reasoning. By utilizing calibrated binocular observations, the model moves beyond semantic priors to ground spatial predictions in explicit cross-view geometry. The architecture employs a hierarchical learning paradigm that progresses from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. The researchers emphasize that disparity supervision provides superior generalization to unseen environments compared to direct binocular depth supervision.

To validate the model, the authors introduced Stereo3D-Bench, a multi-level benchmark covering point-level geometry and object-level spatial reasoning. The StereoVLM-8B variant achieved a 95.17% depth accuracy (δ_1) and a 66.98 average object-level score. Intervention testing confirmed that the model's performance is driven by valid cross-view geometry rather than simply increased visual token counts or semantic priors. Furthermore, the hierarchical geometric supervision approach resulted in a 3.54-point average gain across five spatial benchmarks and a 4.3 percentage point increase in success rates for RoboCasa manipulation tasks.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** StereoVLM-8B utilizes a hierarchical learning approach incorporating cross-view correspondence, disparity estimation, and calibration-conditioned metric depth perception.
**Benchmark Performance:** The model achieved 95.17% depth accuracy (δ_1) and a 66.98 average object-level score on the newly introduced Stereo3D-Bench.
**Supervision Strategy:** Disparity supervision was found to generalize significantly better to unseen environments than direct binocular depth supervision.
**Robotics Impact:** Implementation of hierarchical geometric supervision yielded a 4.3 percentage point improvement in RoboCasa manipulation success rates.
**Validation:** Intervention experiments confirmed that performance gains are derived from cross-view geometric constraints rather than semantic priors or additional visual tokens.

title: Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem
author: Kelly Knight
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 12:46 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026

Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

Agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.’s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control.

That shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Oxide Computer Co., which raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, built its business on the idea that enterprises at scale will want to own their computers, according to Bryan Cantrill (pictured), co-founder and chief technology officer at Oxide.

“Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it. You get to a certain scale, as it turns out, you want to own your own computer,” Cantrill said.

Cantrill spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26 , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed renting versus owning compute, why agentic workloads are moving on-prem and multi-tenancy for isolating those workloads.

Agentic workloads move on-prem

Agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, and much of it is CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. Economics remains the main reason to bring it in-house, but where models live is a close second, Cantrill explained. That makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

“There is a real enterprise drive towards open-weight models, and I think you’re going to see more and more of that as people want to run the models on-prem and allow their data to not actually leave,” Cantrill said.

Security is the other half. Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface, and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. Those early design choices give enterprises a perimeter for isolating agentic workloads, according to Cantrill.

“I think multi-tenancy means you’ve got potentially adversarial tenants that are going to be on the same resource,” Cantrill said. “They’re going to be sharing the same computer, sharing the same network, and they need to do that … without violating the conf

summary.tldr:
Oxide Computer Co. is positioning its on-premises cloud infrastructure as the optimal environment for agentic AI workloads, citing economic and security advantages over public cloud rental models. CTO Bryan Cantrill, speaking at SC26, argued that as enterprises scale, the need to maintain data sovereignty and control over model execution environments drives a shift toward owning hardware. Oxide recently secured $445 million in October to scale its rack production, targeting organizations that require elastic compute capabilities within their own data centers.

Technically, Oxide’s hardware architecture is designed to minimize the attack surface by removing traditional UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controllers. The platform incorporates public cloud-grade multi-tenancy, specifically engineered to isolate potentially adversarial agentic workloads sharing the same physical resources. Beyond AI, the infrastructure is designed to support legacy virtualization workloads, providing a migration path for enterprises seeking alternatives to Broadcom’s VMware pricing models.
takeaways: **Funding:** Oxide Computer Co. raised $445 million in October 2026 to expand its rack production capacity.
**Security Architecture:** Oxide hardware eliminates UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controllers to reduce the attack surface for on-premises deployments.
**Multi-tenancy:** The platform is built to support adversarial multi-tenancy, allowing multiple AI agents to share compute and network resources without compromising data confidentiality.

**Market Positioning:** Oxide is targeting enterprises looking to move away from VMware virtualization while simultaneously hosting open-weight AI models to ensure data remains within the corporate perimeter.

title: RadixArk Ships DaisyRose-27B, a 27B Agentic Coding Model Trained With Reinforcement Learning Only
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: This week RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B , its first open-weight model. DaisyRose-27B is an agentic coding model from RadixArk, post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B with reinforcement learning (RL). The model card page states that it used RL only, with no SFT or distillation. It ships under Apache 2.0 as a drop-in replacement for the base model. The main result: Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 rises from 5.6 to 12.0. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 27.8B dense parameters (0.46B vision encoder, 0.42B MTP head), 262,144-token context. Runs on: 1 GPU. BF16 is about 52 GB, FP8 about 29 GB, NVFP4 about 23 GB (Blackwell only). Listed targets: H200, B200, GB300, RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090, DGX Spark. GGUF also available. Performance: Beats its Qwen3.8-27B base on all 7 reported benchmarks. Best: IFBench 82.4, the top score among the 9 models RadixArk compared. Worst: HLE (text only) 34.3, only +0.4 over the base and below Inkling 2 Small’s 44.1. Bottom line: Best: Terminal Bench 4.1 more than doubles after 18 days of RL. Worst: it still trails much larger MoE models on hard agentic tasks. What is DaisyRose-27B? DaisyRose-27B keeps the Qwen3.8-27B architecture unchanged. The model card lists 64 decoder layers in a 3:1 pattern. Three Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers alternate with 1 full-attention layer. Hidden size is 5,120. A 27-layer vision encoder handles images. One multi-token-prediction layer supports speculative decoding. Input is text and images, output is text, and it is a thinking model. How was DaisyRose-27B trained? RadixArk built about 1,200 curated tasks with Eigent AI , chosen from thousands of candidates. Each task targets a specific failure of the base model. Each sandbox attempt allows up to 1.5 hours, 100+ tool calls and 256k+ output tokens. Agent sessions reach up to 1M tokens, per the blog . Training ran on Miles , RadixArk’s open-source RL framework, in fully asynchronous mode. The run used 144 H200 GPUs for 18 days. Of those, 128 handled agent inference and 16 handled training. Total compute was 63,000 GPU-hours. RadixArk reports 37% MFU on its internal backend. An open-source Megatron-based trainer reached 16%. End-to-end throughput was 16.8k tokens/s versus 8.3k, a 2.0x speedup. RadixArk says this cut GPU time by 57%. Sandboxes ran on AgentENV . RadixArk reports about 94

summary.tldr:
RadixArk has released DaisyRose-27B, an open-weight agentic coding model post-trained exclusively via reinforcement learning (RL) from the Qwen3.8-27B base model. Eschewing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and distillation, the model utilizes a 27.8B dense parameter architecture, including a 0.46B vision encoder and a 0.42B multi-token prediction (MTP) head. It supports a 262,144-token context window and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model is designed as a drop-in replacement for the base Qwen architecture, maintaining 64 decoder layers in a 3:1 Gated DeltaNet linear-attention to full-attention ratio with a hidden size of 5,120.

Training was conducted over 18 days using RadixArk’s open-source 'Miles' RL framework, consuming 63,000 GPU-hours across 144 H200 GPUs. The process utilized 1,200 curated tasks developed with Eigent AI, allowing for sandbox sessions of up to 1.5 hours and 1M tokens. Performance gains are most notable in Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 scores increased from 5.6 to 12.0. While the model outperformed its base on all seven reported benchmarks—including an IFBench score of 82.4—it continues to trail larger Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on complex agentic tasks, specifically recording a 34.3 on the HLE (text-only) benchmark.
takeaways: **Hardware Requirements:** The model runs on a single GPU, with memory footprints of 52 GB (BF16), 29 GB (FP8), and 23 GB (NVFP4, Blackwell-exclusive).

**Training Efficiency:** RadixArk reported 37% Model Flops Utilization (MFU) using their internal backend, achieving a 2.0x throughput increase (16.8k tokens/s) compared to a standard Megatron-based trainer.
**Architecture Specs:** The model features 64 decoder layers, a 27-layer vision encoder, and one MTP layer for speculative decoding, supporting both text and image inputs.
**Benchmark Performance:** Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 more than doubled following the 18-day RL training cycle, though HLE performance remains lower than the Inkling 2 Small model.

title: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
author: Tim Fernholz
contentSnippet:
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?

The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage wil

summary.tldr:
The emerging space-based data center industry faces a significant financial hurdle: the inability to use orbital hardware as loan collateral. Traditional terrestrial data center financing relies on the ability of lenders to repossess and resell chips in the event of a default. According to Compute Credit Index Research, H100 chips retain approximately 50% of their 2023 cost basis, while H200 configurations maintain their original 2024 pricing. Because orbital hardware is inaccessible, lenders involved in SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal reportedly requested that none of the purchased chips be deployed in space, highlighting a fundamental disconnect between space-based infrastructure ambitions and current debt financing models.

SpaceX is currently prioritizing terrestrial compute deployment, with CEO Elon Musk reallocating rocket engineering teams to accelerate ground station build-outs, including internal manufacturing of turbine blades for power generation. While Musk has projected that space will become the most cost-effective location for data centers within two to three years, this remains contingent on achieving full reusability for the Starship launch system. Recent flight tests saw the successful recovery of the orbital stage but failed to recover the booster. Meanwhile, competitors and startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, and Orbital face higher capital costs for hardware compared to terrestrial firms. Google is pursuing a vertical integration strategy via Project Suncatcher to deploy its proprietary TPU chips in orbit, while SpaceX and Tesla’s joint foundry project, Terafab, remains in the pre-construction phase.
takeaways: **Collateral Risk:** Lenders in SpaceX’s $40 billion financing deal reportedly attempted to restrict the use of financed chips in orbital data centers due to the impossibility of asset repossession.
**Hardware Depreciation:** Compute Credit Index Research indicates H100 chips retain roughly 50% of their 2023 cost basis, while H200 units currently trade at their original 2024 launch prices.

**Starship Status:** SpaceX successfully landed the orbital stage of its Starship rocket at its Texas facility during a recent test, but failed to recover the booster stage, leaving the timeline for full reusability uncertain.

**Foundry Ambitions:** The SpaceX and Tesla joint venture, Terafab, aims to establish a U.S.-based semiconductor foundry but has yet to break ground and requires multi-year, multi-billion dollar investment.
**Vertical Integration:** Google is bypassing third-party chip financing constraints for space applications by utilizing its proprietary TPU architecture through Project Suncatcher.

title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
author: Chrisantus Eze
contentSnippet: Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present \sys{}, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs.\ 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], $p = 5.82 \times 10^{-8}$) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0\% vs.\ 15.4\%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta ($\DB$) convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0\% vs.\ 62.5\% for Fixed-$3$) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4$\times$. Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7\% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9\% for a Self-Refine critic, $p = 0.61$) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. Across 200 runs on 40 research hypotheses evaluated with DeepSeek-R1-32B, \sys{} balances compute efficiency with rigorous epistemic verification.

title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
author: Robert Hart
contentSnippet: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field. Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday. The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics. A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof: > I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.” Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. summary.tldr:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician associated with Anthropic, has publicly claimed to have proven the Riemann Hypothesis—a Millennium Prize problem dating back to 1859—using the Claude AI model. Alpöge asserts that his methodology also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and expects it to extend to the Extended Riemann Hypothesis. The proof has been formalized in the Lean programming language and is currently hosted on Alpöge’s personal website. Anthropic has not officially commented on the claim, and the company previously stated in August that it did not expect Claude’s techniques to successfully prove the Riemann Hypothesis.

Verification of the claim remains pending, as the Clay Mathematics Institute requires a two-year period of scrutiny and general acceptance by the global mathematics community before a solution can be considered for the $1 million Millennium Prize. This announcement follows a series of high-profile AI-driven mathematical claims, including OpenAI’s September report regarding the Navier-Stokes problem, which involved the deployment of 10,000 agents and an expenditure of millions of dollars. Alpöge previously claimed to have solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude in July, contributing to a broader trend of AI-assisted research that is currently challenging traditional mathematical workflows.
takeaways: **Millennium Prize Status:** The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, each carrying a $1 million bounty, with only the Poincaré conjecture having been officially solved in the last 25 years.
**Formalization Method:** Alpöge’s proof is presented in the Lean proof assistant language, a standard for formal mathematical verification.

**Verification Requirements:** Per Clay Mathematics Institute rules, any proposed solution must undergo at least two years of public scrutiny and achieve general acceptance within the mathematics community before prize eligibility.
**Prior AI Claims:** Alpöge previously claimed to have solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude in July, while OpenAI recently claimed a solution for the Navier-Stokes problem using 10,000 agents.

title: Anthropic goes public, but is it too late to save the AI trade?
author: Robert Hof
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026

Anthropic goes public, but is it too late to save the AI trade?

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?

The artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success. But it seemed to take some of the air out of AI stocks. Continued worries over AI spending and prospects, as well as factors such as a likely interest-rate hike, dragged down the entire market, including other AI names from Google, Microsoft and Meta to AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia.

No doubt Anthropic stock will be at least as volatile as other AI stocks, but it can live with that alongside the more than $90 billion in its bank account. Now all eyes turn to OpenAI, which finds itself chasing after Anthropic in more ways than one, with plans to go public sometime in next year.

Nvidia posted its usual better-than-expected earnings this week, which didn’t help its stock much but indicates, along with interim CEO Colette Kress’ bullish comments during the earnings call, that it’s going to be fine in disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang’s absence.

Meantime, Huang said he’s open to returning — but that’s not only appallingly premature, the board appears adamant that’s not going to happen. The supposed friends clamoring for his return are just reinforcing their selfish, clueless nature, the attitude that has plunged tech into such low esteem that auto salespeople and journalists have more company now. Maybe those guys (always guys) approve of behavior like this .

What’s with all the outages all over the place? That’s what everyone’s asking, and we looked into what’s behind them all. It doesn’t seem to be the obvious thing — cybersecurity attacks — or really any single cause. Perhaps it’s a lot of 20th century technologies that just aren’t ready for the AI-driven speed of the 21st century, making everything less reliable. On the other hand, is it only a coincidence that the U.S. cyber director just got canned this week?

Palo Alto Networks remains one of the most acquisitive cybersecurity companies out there, once again laying out a tidy sum this week, buying AI startup Applied Compute this week $4.5 bill

summary.tldr:
Anthropic successfully completed its initial public offering on Thursday, November 19, 2026, with shares rising 17% on the first day of trading. The company enters the public markets with over $90 billion in cash reserves. The IPO performance, while positive, coincided with a broader market decline in AI-related equities, including major players like Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and Meta, amid investor concerns regarding AI spending sustainability and potential interest-rate hikes. OpenAI is reportedly planning its own IPO for 2027.

In other industry developments, Palo Alto Networks acquired AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion, signaling continued consolidation in the cybersecurity sector. Nvidia held its first earnings call following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang, with interim CEO Colette Kress reporting better-than-expected results. Meanwhile, the AI model landscape saw significant updates, including OpenAI's release of GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Google's launch of the mid-tier Gemini 4 Neon model, and Alibaba's introduction of Qwen4-Max.
takeaways: **Anthropic IPO:** Shares rose 17% on the first day of trading, with the company holding over $90 billion in cash.
**Cybersecurity M&A:** Palo Alto Networks acquired AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion.
**Model Releases:** OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra (professional) and Sol (everyday); Google released Gemini 4 Neon, which is reportedly three times faster than the Carbon model.
**Nvidia Leadership:** Interim CEO Colette Kress led the company's first earnings call post-Jensen Huang, reporting results that exceeded market expectations.
**Funding Rounds:** Isomorphic Labs raised $5 billion for AI-driven drug discovery, while Model ML secured $250 million at a $1.5 billion valuation.

Despite the leadership transition, the company reported healthy earnings growth and provided positive forward-looking guidance. title: Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and Practical Multilingual Translation Models in the Wild
author: Mao Zheng
contentSnippet: Hy-MT3 is the third generation of the Hunyuan multilingual translation model family, including \textbf{Hy-MT3-1.8B}, \textbf{Hy-MT3-7B} and \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (MoE)}. Compared with Hy-MT2, Hy-MT3 translates \textbf{more accurately, more completely and more faithfully to user constraints}: on real-world scenario data, the share of samples with mistranslations is reduced by \textbf{43\%}, omissions or additions by \textbf{74\%}, and instruction-following errors by \textbf{40\%}, while language coverage is expanded from \textbf{38 to 102} languages. With only 3B activated parameters, \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models in non-thinking mode}, including flagship models such as Qwen3.8-Max, Kimi-K3.1-Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and approaches the strongest closed-source thinking models such as GPT-6.1-Sol and Gemini-4-Argon, while surpassing models that consume \textbf{more than 30$\times$} its inference compute. Beyond general translation, Hy-MT3 is optimized for two industrial scenarios. For \textbf{game localization}, built with high-quality game-domain data and a professional evaluation system from the Honor of Kings team, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B matches or outperforms strong closed-source models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro on all core metrics, and can be plugged into game development pipelines through an open-source toolchain. For \textbf{image translation}, Hy-MT3 improves context understanding and error correction to better tolerate OCR errors, achieving the best result among models of comparable size. Finally, we open-source \textbf{TransRubric}, a rubric-based automatic evaluation suite for translation, which outperforms other evaluation schemes on the WMT26 metrics shared task test set and is more stable with respect to human evaluation.

title: NVIDIA AI Releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a Continuous Diffusion Language Model with 14 checkpoints at 3B/8B
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA has released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma , a collection of 14 open checkpoints at 3B and 8B scale. Nemotron-Labs-Sigma is a continuous diffusion language model family that denoises text in a 16-D embedding space. Most diffusion LLMs, such as LLaDA and Dream, work on discrete tokens. Sigma works in a smooth latent space instead. NVIDIA team states that this makes few-step distillation and trajectory steering practical for text. TL;DR Size: 3B and 8B parameters, 14 checkpoints. Context is 4,096 tokens (8,192 for Sigma-8B-instruct). Runs on: 1 NVIDIA GPU in bfloat16 (Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper, Blackwell). About 120 to 140 tokens/s on 1 H100. No CPU support, no quantized variants listed. Performance: Sigma-8B base averages 71.16 on NVIDIA’s 6-task suite, ahead of NLD-8B (70.22). Best: 91.96 on GSM8K (Sigma-8B-instruct, 256 DDPM steps). Worst: 17.00 on AIME25 (same model and sampler). Bottom line: Best: the 8-step distilled 8B keeps a 70.34 average. Worst: the instruct average (59.14) trails NLD-8B (59.92). What is Nemotron-Labs-Sigma? The research team calls Sigma the first large-scale family of continuous diffusion language models. The collection has 4 variant types at each size: Base: Sigma-3B and Sigma-8B. Instruct: Sigma-3B-instruct and Sigma-8B-instruct. Few-step distilled: distill-3B and distill-8B at NFE 2, 4, 8 and 16 (8 checkpoints). Self-speculative: distill-spec-3B and distill-spec-8B. How does continuous diffusion for language work? Each token maps to a point in a learned 16-D embedding space . Training adds Gaussian noise to these embeddings and teaches the model to remove it. The embedding geometry is learned jointly with the denoiser. Generation runs blockwise. Each denoised block is committed to a KV cache before the next starts. Blocks default to 64 tokens. The backbone is a Ministral-style decoder-only Transformer with grouped-query attention, SwiGLU and rotary embeddings. Training starts from an autoregressive warm start of about 1T tokens. About 0.3T tokens of diffusion training follow. At inference, classifier-free guidance and score temperature matter most. The model card page recommends guidance 3 and temperature 0.3 at 32 DDIM steps. Why does a continuous space matter? Discrete diffusion jumps between token states, so its trajectories are hard to steer. Sigma follows smooth ODE/SDE paths instead. Per the research paper , these degrade grace

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a family of continuous diffusion language models available in 3B and 8B parameter sizes across 14 distinct checkpoints. Unlike discrete diffusion models such as LLaDA or Dream, Sigma operates by denoising text within a learned 16-dimensional continuous embedding space. This architectural shift allows for smooth trajectory steering and practical few-step distillation. The models utilize a Ministral-style decoder-only Transformer backbone featuring grouped-query attention, SwiGLU, and rotary embeddings, initialized with a 1T token autoregressive warm start followed by 0.3T tokens of diffusion training.

Performance metrics show the Sigma-8B base model achieving a 71.16 average across NVIDIA’s 6-task suite, outperforming the NLD-8B model at 70.22. The Sigma-8B-instruct variant peaks at 91.96 on GSM8K using 256 DDPM steps, though it trails NLD-8B in overall instruct averages (59.14 vs 59.92). The model supports a 4,096-token context window, extending to 8,192 for the 8B-instruct version. Inference requires a single NVIDIA GPU (Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper, or Blackwell) in bfloat16 precision, yielding approximately 120 to 140 tokens/s on an H100. No CPU support or quantized variants are currently provided.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** Employs a continuous diffusion process in a 16-D embedding space, utilizing a blockwise generation strategy with 64-token blocks committed to a KV cache.
**Checkpoint Variety:** Includes base, instruct, few-step distilled (NFE 2, 4, 8, 16), and self-speculative variants for both 3B and 8B sizes.
**Inference Requirements:** Requires bfloat16 precision on NVIDIA GPUs; recommended settings include classifier-free guidance of 3 and a score temperature of 0.3 at 32 DDIM steps.
**Performance Benchmarks:** Sigma-8B-instruct achieves 91.96 on GSM8K, while the 8-step distilled 8B model maintains a 70.34 average across the 6-task suite.

title: The week everything fell apart
author: David Pierce
contentSnippet: There was a dayslong Outlook outage. A nationwide ground stop for only the second time in 25 years. Banks seemed to suddenly stop working. Even iCloud couldn’t stay up and running. This week, it felt like the technological world simply collapsed. And it felt like this might be the beginning of something even bigger. On this episode of The Vergecast, Nilay and David go through the week’s many calamities, and try to explain both what happened in each case — which was generally much milder than the conspiracy theories would have you believe — and why all these small issues might still add up to something worth worrying about. In a world filled with more AI and fewer humans, we’re going to see new kinds of problems and often struggle to find the fixes. After that, the hosts discuss the latest in the Jensen Huang / Nvidia scandal, which is increasingly less about affairs and more about the allegedly very big business of illegally smuggling chips to China. Huang will not be back as Nvidia CEO anytime soon, no matter what a bunch of X users want, and the fallout of his exit seems likely to only increase. Finally, in the lightning round, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, Nilay’s experience with his always-listening Apple Watch, Google’s inability to name products, and much more. Watch | Listen | Get ad-free In case you missed it this week: We also talked about e-readers, computer chips, GTA VI, and the world after GTA VI. And we want to hear all your thoughts about all of it! Call the Hotline at 866-VERGE11, send us an email at vergecast@theverge.com, and tell us everything that’s on your mind. And make sure you subscribe so you don’t miss an episode!

summary.tldr:
This episode of The Vergecast, hosted by Nilay Patel and David Pierce, analyzes a series of high-profile technological service disruptions that occurred within a single week, including outages affecting Microsoft Outlook, iCloud, and a nationwide ground stop. The hosts argue that while individual incidents were less severe than public speculation suggested, the cumulative frequency of these failures highlights systemic vulnerabilities in an increasingly automated, AI-driven infrastructure where human oversight is diminishing.

The discussion shifts to Nvidia, specifically addressing the ongoing controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang. The hosts clarify that the situation has evolved beyond personal allegations to focus on the significant business implications of illegal chip smuggling to China. They emphasize that Huang’s departure as CEO is definitive, despite social media speculation to the contrary, and suggest that the resulting corporate fallout is expected to intensify.
takeaways: **Service Disruptions:** The week featured a rare nationwide ground stop, alongside widespread outages for Microsoft Outlook and Apple's iCloud services.
**Nvidia Leadership:** The podcast confirms Jensen Huang will not return as Nvidia CEO, with the primary focus of the scandal shifting toward the illicit export of chips to China.
**Systemic Risk:** The hosts posit that the transition toward AI-heavy, human-light systems creates novel failure modes that are increasingly difficult to diagnose and repair.
**Editorial Commentary:** The episode includes segments on FCC Commissioner Brendan Carr, Apple Watch privacy concerns, and Google’s product naming strategies.

title: Report2Alpha-Bench: Evaluating LLM Agents on End-to-End Quantitative Research
author: Yun Zhang
contentSnippet: We evaluate whether LLM agents can independently carry out a several-hour quantitative research project: read a brokerage research report, make a plan, and over 7 rounds of iteration propose hypotheses, write factor code and improve it from backtest feedback, seeing only 2022-2023 market data. Like Terminal-Bench-Science, the task evaluates overall research ability; unlike it, there is no directly checkable unique answer: the model must repeatedly propose hypotheses on very noisy data, revise its understanding from experiments, disentangle multiple factors and design ablations without overfitting in-sample, much like complex real-world decisions with many interacting factors. After the research, a fixed rule using only 2022-2023 results selects a low-correlated factor pool from all candidates the model produced, and scores it on unseen 2024-2025 data after removing common style returns such as size and momentum; the same rule on round-0 candidates alone gives a report baseline that "implements the report without iterating". We run gpt-6.1-sol (reasoning effort xhigh), gpt-6.1-terra (xhigh), muse-spark-1.3 (xhigh) and deepseek-v4.1-flash (max) once on each of 7 reports. Of the 28 runs, 19 factor pools pass the usability threshold; the average score is 48.4 (0-100 scale), against 25.4 for the report baseline and 35.9 for the models' own picks. From similar report baselines (17.0-31.0), the models separate after iteration to 74.7 (gpt-6.1-sol), 56.6 (gpt-6.1-terra), 35.8 (deepseek-v4.1-flash) and 26.2 (muse-spark-1.3); their candidates look equally good in training and diverge only in testing, with the leaders proposing more diverse ideas per round and ending with more effective factors in the pool. Evaluating research agents thus requires scoring on frozen future data after removing styles, and measuring "what the research produced" separately from "what was finally picked".

We run gpt-6.1-sol (reasoning effort xhigh), gpt-6.1-terra (xhigh), muse-spark-1.3 (xhigh) and deepseek-v4.1-flash (max) once on each of 7 reports. From similar report baselines (17.0-31.0), the models separate after iteration to 74.7 (gpt-6.1-sol), 56.6 (gpt-6.1-terra), 35.8 (deepseek-v4.1-flash) and 26.2 (muse-spark-1.3); their candidates look equally good in training and diverge only in testing, with the leaders proposing more diverse ideas per round and ending with more effective factors in the pool.
takeaways: Evaluating research agents thus requires scoring on frozen future data after removing styles, and measuring "what the research produced" separately from "what was finally picked".

title: Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter
author: Lauren Forristal
contentSnippet:
Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.

From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.

Flowtica Scribe Pen ($159)

If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, Flowtica’s Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.

The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.

You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.

The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.

Anker Soundcore Work ($159)

Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.

Priced at $159, the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to five meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.

The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month.

If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).

Logitech MX Keypad ($99)

Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier.

The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative

This briefing covers six hardware products integrating AI for home office productivity, ranging from transcription tools to smart furniture. The Flowtica Scribe Pen ($159) and Anker Soundcore Work ($159) focus on meeting capture; the Scribe Pen features 32GB storage, 15-speaker identification, and 92-language support, while the Soundcore Work offers an 8-hour battery (32 hours with case) and 300 minutes of free monthly transcription. Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($629) targets professionals with AI-driven handwriting cleanup, document summarization, and cross-note search capabilities.

Productivity and environmental hardware include the Logitech MX Keypad ($99), which provides dedicated physical shortcuts for tools like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Adobe Creative Suite. The Insta360 Link 2 Pro ($249) is a 4K webcam utilizing AI for intelligent subject tracking, group framing, and noise cancellation. Finally, the Autonomous Desk Pro ($599) functions as an AI-monitored standing desk that tracks user posture, suggests movement intervals, and monitors environmental metrics such as CO2 levels.
takeaways: **Flowtica Scribe Pen:** Features 32GB onboard storage, supports 92 languages, and identifies up to 15 distinct speakers during audio transcription.
**Anker Soundcore Work:** Provides a 5-meter recording range with a base subscription model offering 300 free minutes of transcription monthly, with Pro ($99/yr) and Unlimited ($239/yr) tiers.
**Logitech MX Keypad:** Configurable for specific AI and productivity workflows, including GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Microsoft 365 apps.
**Insta360 Link 2 Pro:** A 4K webcam featuring AI-based automatic framing, group tracking, and integrated noise cancellation for video conferencing.
**Autonomous Desk Pro:** Uses integrated sensors to track sitting/standing ratios and room CO2 levels, providing activity insights via an AI interface.

title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
author: Jess Weatherbed
contentSnippet: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access. “We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.” Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed

summary.tldr:
Signal is implementing a restrictive policy on Android and iOS to block screenshot capabilities, aiming to prevent OS-level AI agents like Google Gemini and Apple’s Siri from scraping user messages. Signal President Meredith Whittaker stated that current operating system architectures allow AI agents to access on-screen data, which fundamentally undermines the app's privacy guarantees. While users can manually re-enable screenshots in the app settings, Signal warns that this action exposes message content to AI analysis and voids the platform's privacy protections.

Signal characterizes the current OS-level integration of AI as an 'existential threat' to application-layer privacy, noting that developers lack granular tools to restrict AI access without degrading core user experiences. The company specifically cited the inability to implement these protections on macOS due to a lack of developer-facing controls. Signal is calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide standardized technical tools and transparent documentation regarding how AI agents interact with application data, specifically highlighting concerns over accessibility settings being used as a 'skeleton key' for data extraction. This move follows Signal's previous efforts to block Microsoft’s Recall feature from accessing encrypted chats.
takeaways: **Core Mechanism:** Signal is disabling screenshot functionality on Android and iOS to prevent AI assistants from reading on-screen content.

**Developer Limitations:** Signal reports that major OS providers (Google, Apple, Microsoft) fail to provide robust APIs for developers to restrict AI data access without compromising app functionality.
**Platform Disparity:** The screenshot-blocking protection is currently unavailable on macOS due to the lack of necessary developer controls provided by Apple.
**Security Warning:** Signal explicitly warns that re-enabling screenshot capabilities in app settings will expose user data to AI agents and break the app's privacy guarantees.

**Industry Advocacy:** Signal is demanding that OS vendors provide 'simple technical tools' and documentation to prevent third-party agents from using accessibility settings to bypass application-level security.

title: Combatting adversarial distillation
author: OpenAI News
contentSnippet:
November 20, 2026 Combatting adversarial distillation How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

W e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming , we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Why distillation is a safety issue

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answ

summary.tldr:
OpenAI detailed its methods for combatting adversarial distillation, a process where malicious actors extract frontier model capabilities and internal reasoning traces to train unprotected student models. Focusing on dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology, the company outlined risks where transferred skills enable offensive capabilities previously blocked by original model safeguards.

To counter protected reasoning extraction, OpenAI updated its defenses in GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal adaptive evaluations using automated red-teaming, the attack success rate dropped from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra with original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with updated safeguards. The defense architecture spans request-level controls—including adversarial training, input/output classifiers covering tool-call arguments, and API-level restrictions tying encrypted reasoning to specific conversation histories—and campaign-level investigations tracking coordinated extraction patterns across user and organization boundaries.
takeaways: **Red-Teaming Benchmark Improvement:** The average attack success rate for recovering protected reasoning fell from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with updated safeguards during internal adaptive evaluations.
**Model Generations Evaluated:** The defense updates and evaluations specifically target the GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol model families.

**Exact Reasoning vs. Summaries:** Internal studies showed that student models fine-tuned on exact reasoning traces outperformed students trained on reasoning summaries after supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

**API and Tool-Call Safeguards:** Output classifiers scan both assistant messages and tool-call arguments to prevent reasoning leakage, while API controls tie encrypted reasoning strictly to its originating conversation history and prevent older model families from reading GPT-6.2 reasoning.

title: SAVIOR: Sample-efficient Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for OCR Representation
author: Akshata A Bhat
contentSnippet: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) pipelines and vision-language models exhibit high accuracy on standard OCR and document-understanding benchmarks, yet they systematically underperform on document patterns that are operationally critical in financial workflows. These patterns include vertical or rotated text, logo-embedded vendor names, fine-print regulatory clauses, degraded scans, and complex multi-column layouts. While underrepresented in public datasets, they constitute a substantial portion of real-world failure cases. We introduce SAVIOR, a sample-efficient data curation methodology that targets such high-impact failure scenarios to adapt vision-language models for robust financial OCR. We further propose PaIRS, a structure-aware evaluation metric that measures layout fidelity by comparing pairwise spatial relationships between tokens. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct with SAVIOR-Train achieves a word recall of 0.93. When the resulting layout-aware OCR output is used as context for document question answering, it attains an F1 score of 0.89, outperforming both open- and closed-source models such as GPT-4o, Mistral-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, and DeepSeek-OCR.

title: HookEvo: A Framework for Coordinated Plugin Evolution on Hook-Enabled Agent Runtimes
author: Shengze Huang
contentSnippet: Repairing failures in tool-using agents can require coordinated changes to how the harness interprets tool receipts, assembles context, and checks actions. We introduce HookEvo, a framework that uses an existing agent runtime's lifecycle hooks to evolve task-specific harnesses. We instantiate HookEvo on DeepSeek Harness. In each round, a separate improver diagnoses failures from execution traces and proposes a candidate. HookEvo evaluates the candidate against the current harness on matched tasks and carries the retained version into the next round. A single candidate can jointly edit executable plugin handlers and the state they share within a task, allowing a tool receipt to inform context and control a later action. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B executor, the selected harnesses lead the reported Qwen3-4B comparisons, achieving 95.41% on ALFWorld, 70.56% on DBBench, 48.17% on WebShop, and 41.67% on OSBench. Across three improvers and three edit scopes, from skill text to single-component and coordinated executable edits, GPT-6.1 Sol shows the largest average gain from the broadest scope. Our code is available at https://huangshengzebluesky.github.io/hookevo/.

title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting
author: Jingyi Chai
contentSnippet: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. To address these, we introduce a forecasting training framework including harness design and post-training. For the harness side, we propose Proactive Belief-State Management (PBM), equipping agents with a fold tool to compress lengthy context into compact belief states and reset the context for subsequent exploration. For the training side, we develop SEIPH, a five-dimensional, outcome-blind rubric, providing process-quality rewards. Using the rubric-based reward, we post-train a 35B model with PPO and GRPO, yielding DeepForecaster-PPO and DeepForecaster-GRPO. Theoretically, we prove that idealized fold-based stopping converges and calibrated local rewards reduce segment-level gradient variance. Empirically, DeepForecaster-PPO (35B) achieves the best Brier score on both ForecastBench and Polymarket-Sim, outperforming frontier agents based on DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T), Kimi-K2.6 (1T), and GPT-5.5. DeepForecaster-GRPO ranks second on both FutureX metrics. Ablations reveal that PBM also improves the untrained base model without any training. Calibration analysis shows that DeepForecaster-PPO makes more accurate high-confidence predictions than Qwen3.6 and GPT-5.5. Trajectory analysis further shows that forecasts generally improve from the first to the final belief state as agents gather evidence and revise their judgments.

title: LongCat Recall Sparse Attention: Co-Designing Key Organization and Retrieval for Long-Context Inference
author: Hao Zhang
contentSnippet: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. To address this problem, we propose LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA), which combines fine-grained representatives with paged retrieval in an incrementally maintained index. LRSA partitions the sequence into time buckets that can be indexed independently as new keys arrive, without regrouping existing history. Within each bucket, it organizes indexing keys into capacity-balanced directional groups and packs a fixed number of complete groups into each page, retaining a separate center for every group. These centers provide fine-grained representatives for page selection, after which refinement scores members of the selected pages together with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates to select the final Top-$K$ logical positions. To execute this retrieval process efficiently, we store members in reordered pages, fuse construction stages according to group size, and share storage for overlapping fixed candidates across queries during chunked prefill. These choices support regular member access while reducing kernel launches during construction and repeated candidate transfers. Moreover, we integrate LRSA into SGLang to maintain the index during inference, overlapping asynchronous index construction for new buckets with subsequent computation and reusing compatible bucket indices and member pages after a prefix match in the original key-value pool. With a 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection by 4.70$\times$ over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60$\times$ over full attention.

title: EDAGoat: An EDA-Aware Agent for Project-Level GPU Optimization
author: Chengxi Li
contentSnippet: GPU acceleration has transformed electronic design automation (EDA), yet further improving expert-engineered GPU tools still demands substantial manual effort. Automating this work calls for coding agents that can trace bottlenecks across host and device code while preserving correctness and design quality. We introduce EDAGoat, to our knowledge the first EDA-aware GPU optimization agent for this task. Its optimization enhancement (OE) mode guides edits with four cross-project GPU optimization patterns. Its mandatory validation (MV) mode requires the agent to test the edited program against the EDA constraints its changes could affect. Our benchmark covers five GPU EDA projects across four task families and 55 circuit inputs, measuring complete-solve runtime and verifying the resulting designs. Each configuration runs three independent searches per project. A search qualifies only if its solver passes correctness and design-quality checks on all public and hidden inputs. With DeepSeek, generic prompting qualifies in 7 of 15 searches and OE in 6 of 15, despite a higher best speedup on four projects. Adding MV raises this to 13 of 15 and, on every project, exceeds both generic baselines in mean and best speedup and OE in mean speedup; the geometric mean of per-project mean speedups rises from 1.11x (1.36x with OE) to 1.53x. With GPT-6 Astra, EDAGoat qualifies in all 15 searches and improves both speedup metrics over generic prompting on every project, lifting the same geometric mean from 1.26x to 1.57x. These results show that agents can use EDA knowledge to find further speedups in expert-tuned tools while preserving design correctness and quality, establishing EDA-aware GPU optimization as a new direction for agent research.

Its optimization enhancement (OE) mode guides edits with four cross-project GPU optimization patterns. Its mandatory validation (MV) mode requires the agent to test the edited program against the EDA constraints its changes could affect. Our benchmark covers five GPU EDA projects across four task families and 55 circuit inputs, measuring complete-solve runtime and verifying the resulting designs.
