title: Google adds computer use capabilities to Gemini’s Mac app
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:41 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026

Google adds computer use capabilities to Gemini’s Mac app

Google LLC today released a new version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

The feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

Users can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project plan and carries out the work step by step.

The assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

Gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

The AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, users don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

“Privacy and safety are built in: you choose which apps Gemini can access, watch every step live, pause at any time, and approve key actions before they happen,” Michael Friedman, Google’s group product manager for the Gemini app, wrote in a blog post .

The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently launched AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

Google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The company can also extend Gemini in other wa

summary.tldr:
Google has released an update to its Gemini Mac application that introduces "computer use" capabilities, allowing the AI to interact directly with local applications and web services. Available currently in the U.S. for Google AI subscription holders, the feature is triggered by the "@Computer use" command. The assistant is designed to handle complex, multi-step workflows, such as transforming a sketch into a 3D animation or moving data between local software and cloud services, by creating and executing a step-by-step project plan.

Technically, the assistant operates in a background window, allowing users to continue working while Gemini executes tasks. Users can monitor progress via a preview pane in the chat interface and provide real-time feedback. Privacy controls allow users to specify which applications the AI can access, view steps live, pause execution, and manually approve key actions before they occur. This release positions Gemini to compete with similar agentic offerings, such as Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, which also feature local application integration and, in some cases, cloud-based virtual machine support for offline task execution.
takeaways: **Activation Command:** Users initiate the computer use mode by typing "@Computer use" within the Gemini Mac client prompts.
**Privacy Controls:** The system requires user-defined permissions for app access and includes manual approval gates for key actions during task execution.

**Workflow Capabilities:** Gemini can chain multiple actions across different applications, such as generating a visual asset in a design tool and subsequently converting it into a mini-app using Visual Studio Code.
**Competitive Landscape:** The feature directly competes with Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, both of which offer similar local application interaction capabilities.
**Subscription Requirement:** Access is restricted to users with a paid Google AI subscription, which also includes additional storage and other premium features.

title: Resolve AI’s SRE-1 model finds root causes of production alerts as AI agents go on call
author: Duncan Riley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:11 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026

Resolve AI’s SRE-1 model finds root causes of production alerts as AI agents go on call

Incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc. has announced the launch of SRE-1, a new model that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, and Primary On-call, a new service that puts its artificial intelligence agents on call ahead of human engineers.

The new model, announced Wednesday, reflects the company’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run. According to Resolve AI, production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private.

SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, which used reinforcement learning alone, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%.

Resolve AI used Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training , a serverless service for customizing open-weight models, to build SRE-1. Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan said Resolve AI was the first design partner for the service.

In testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations, solving about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents.

Primary On-call puts that research to work on the critical path. Each page is investigated across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, according to the company. Depending on what it finds, the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team’s policies permit or escalate to a human. Once it has acted, the agent checks the fix against the production baseline, monitoring it until recovery holds.

The agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem. For teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page.

Up to 80% of paged alerts in p

summary.tldr:
Resolve AI Inc. has launched SRE-1, a 27-billion parameter model specifically engineered for production incident remediation, alongside a new service called Primary On-call that deploys AI agents to handle production alerts. The model was trained by a team of 16 researchers over 7.4 days using up to 512 GPUs, leveraging Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training service. Unlike general-purpose coding models, SRE-1 was trained using reinforcement learning on private production incident data, which the company identifies as a critical gap in current AI training corpora.

Technically, SRE-1 demonstrated a significant performance jump in single-investigation pass rates, increasing from 6.9% to 38.8% post-training. In benchmarks involving 178 production alert investigations, the system reportedly solved twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents. When deployed via Primary On-call, the agent integrates telemetry, infrastructure, code, and operational knowledge to either resolve, mitigate, or escalate alerts. The system includes a 'shadow mode' for teams to audit agent decisions before full automation, and it is capable of monitoring fixes against production baselines until recovery is confirmed.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** SRE-1 is a 27-billion parameter model trained via reinforcement learning on private production incident data.
**Performance Metrics:** The model achieved a 38.8% pass rate for single investigations, up from 6.9% pre-training, and claims up to 95% root-cause accuracy.
**Operational Impact:** Primary On-call is reported to handle up to 80% of production alerts without human escalation, with early users like Salesforce reporting a 70% reduction in paging alerts.
**Company Status:** Resolve AI has raised over $190 million, with a $1.5 billion valuation following a $40 million Series A extension in April 2026.
**Availability:** SRE-1 is currently restricted to the Resolve AI platform, while the Primary On-call service is now generally available.

title: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments
author: Madhu Samhitha Vangara
contentSnippet: When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace , so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys. Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the new AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer . Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect. The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them: Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them. That conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale. This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like. — Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily What’s launching today Today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill. When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a succe

summary.tldr:
Amazon has expanded its Bedrock AgentCore payments infrastructure to support direct purchasing from the AWS Marketplace using the x402 protocol. This integration allows AI agents to autonomously discover and purchase x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, with transactions settled directly in USD on the developer’s AWS bill. By eliminating the requirement for stablecoin wallets or manual API key management, the system aims to facilitate enterprise-grade agentic commerce while maintaining existing security and auditability standards.

Technically, the workflow utilizes the AgentCore Gateway and its AWS Marketplace connector to automate discovery and purchasing. When a seller returns a '402 Payment Required' response, it includes a signed quote that the agent forwards to AgentCore payments. The system validates the request against pre-configured session budgets and spending limits before issuing a payment token, which the agent then uses to complete the transaction. All activity is logged via AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer, ensuring that agentic spending remains visible and controllable within standard enterprise financial workflows.
takeaways: **Protocol Support:** The system utilizes the x402 and MPP open protocols to facilitate autonomous agent payments.
**Billing Integration:** Agent purchases are settled in USD directly through the developer's AWS bill, removing the need for cryptocurrency or external payment methods.
**Governance Controls:** Developers can enforce spending limits, define approved sellers via AgentCore policy, and utilize session caps to prevent unauthorized overspending.
**Auditability:** All transactions are natively integrated with AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer for enterprise-grade monitoring.
**Partner Ecosystem:** Tavily is an early participant in the x402-enabled AWS Marketplace, focusing on providing live search capabilities for agentic commerce.

title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
author: Emma Roth
contentSnippet: Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That's according to a now-removed job listing spotted by Bloomberg , which said Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant. An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta's Muse , OpenAI's Dots , Anthropic's Duet , and Google's Tasks . Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same. Apple began ro … Read the full story at The Verge.

summary.tldr:
Apple is actively recruiting for a lead engineer to develop agentic AI capabilities, aiming to expand its current AI infrastructure into a system capable of executing multi-step tasks across browsers, terminals, code editors, and APIs. The initiative, identified via a recent job posting, seeks to integrate these agents with Apple’s existing Siri, UI Frameworks, and Foundation Models divisions. This effort positions Apple to compete directly with emerging agentic frameworks from rivals, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks, all of which are increasingly focused on cross-application control.

Technically, the project aims to enable AI to coordinate specialized sub-agents to perform complex workflows that span multiple software environments. This builds upon Apple's existing AI-upgraded Siri, which currently supports screen-context awareness and basic cross-app actions. Future iterations are expected to include granular tasks such as image manipulation in Photos and Safari tab management. Furthermore, Apple is expanding developer access through a Developer Preview in iOS 27.3, which allows for Siri AI integration across third-party applications, signaling a broader push toward system-wide agentic interoperability.
takeaways: **Strategic Hiring:** Apple is seeking a lead engineer to build agents capable of planning and executing multi-step tasks across browsers, command lines, and APIs.
**Internal Integration:** The agentic development team will collaborate directly with Apple’s Siri, UI Frameworks, and Foundation Models divisions.
**Competitive Landscape:** The project is a direct response to agentic AI developments from competitors including Meta (Muse), OpenAI (Dots), Anthropic (Duet), and Google (Tasks).

title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
author: Dr. Jens Kohl
contentSnippet: When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought. At the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high. While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge. Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group. In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance. Solution Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain. Central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation. Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start. We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified a

summary.tldr:
The BMW Group is scaling agentic AI across its R&D division, which supports over 12,500 developers managing 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This infrastructure integrates with the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system comprising more than 1,300 microservices that serve 24 million vehicles globally. To manage the deployment of hundreds of agents across distributed teams, BMW is implementing a governance strategy designed to balance developer autonomy with enterprise-wide requirements for safety, security, and cost-efficiency.

Central to BMW's approach is the 'agent harness,' a runtime layer that wraps around LLMs to manage execution loops, tool dispatch, memory, and observability. Rather than mandating a single framework or toolchain, the organization utilizes reusable blueprints that encode governance and composability standards. This architecture aims to prevent the formation of fragmented 'AI islands' and redundant development efforts by ensuring that agents are built to cooperate from the outset, following patterns established by the company's internal agentic systems development since 2023.
takeaways: **Scale Metrics:** BMW R&D manages 500 million lines of code with 12,500 developers and a backend of 1,300+ microservices.
**Fleet Reach:** The BMW Connected Vehicle backend currently supports 24 million active vehicles in the field.
**Technical Architecture:** The 'agent harness' provides the core runtime layer for LLMs, handling tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks.
**Governance Strategy:** BMW utilizes reusable blueprints to enforce standards for safety, security, and composability without restricting teams to a single toolchain.

title: A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
author: Ellen Thomas
contentSnippet: “We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call. By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected. Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors. “Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.” But investors are still trying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future. The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times. Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on. It has been a tumultuous two an

summary.tldr:
Nvidia is navigating a period of extreme volatility following the resignation of co-founder and long-time CEO Jensen Huang. The leadership transition, triggered by an independent board investigation into Huang’s extramarital affairs and potential national security risks involving a Chinese espionage plot, has seen the company's stock price drop to a 52-week low of $145.98. Interim CEO Colette Kress is currently managing the company, with board chairman Harvey Jones confirming that the firm has engaged an executive search firm to identify a permanent successor. Despite the leadership crisis, Nvidia reported a strong third quarter, with revenue doubling year-over-year to $115.8 billion, bolstered by a 110 percent increase in data center revenue and the successful launch of the Vera Rubin platform, which generated $20 billion in revenue.

While financial fundamentals remain robust, the company faces significant external pressures, including upcoming congressional testimony before the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees scheduled for early December. Investors are also weighing the impact of regulatory uncertainty, potential shifts in data center construction policies, and the long-term implications of the leadership vacuum. Despite the turmoil, analyst sentiment remains largely positive, with nearly two-thirds of analysts maintaining a "Buy" rating and an average price target of $232.59. Retail investors have shown significant interest in the volatility, recording $111 million in share purchases during the first 30 minutes of trading on the day of Huang’s departure.
takeaways: **Financial Performance:** Nvidia reported Q3 revenue of $115.8 billion, with data center revenue growing 110% year-over-year.
**Product Milestone:** The Vera Rubin platform contributed $20 billion in revenue, marking the fastest product ramp in the company's history.
**Leadership Transition:** Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following an investigation into personal conduct; the board has explicitly stated it does not intend to reinstate him.
**Market Impact:** Nvidia shares hit a 52-week low of $145.98 on November 12th, representing a nearly 40% drop from the October 6th all-time high.
**Regulatory Scrutiny:** Nvidia leadership is scheduled to provide testimony to the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on December 1st and 2nd.

title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet: Posted: 1:58 PM PST · November 19, 2026 Image Credits: Meta/screenshot / Lucas Ropek Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300 Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported . When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality. Muse Charm, the company’s push into AI hardware, will allow users to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands. It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin ), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience. Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-new Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm. summary.tldr:
Meta is reportedly planning to price its upcoming Muse Charm AI wearable at $300, according to a report from The Information. First teased at Meta’s Connect event earlier this year, the device is designed as a physical, portable companion for the company’s existing 'Muse' agentic software. takeaways: **Product Pricing:** Meta’s Muse Charm is expected to retail for $300.
**Form Factor:** The device is a keychain-sized wearable intended for pocket or neck-worn use, serving as a physical interface for Meta’s Muse agentic AI.
**Competitive Context:** The $300 price point exceeds the $250 Friend AI wearable and significantly outprices the $75 Amazon Bee Frontier.
**Meta's Stance:** Meta has neither confirmed nor denied the pricing, stating they will have more information to share in the future.

title: Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Meta FAIR has introduced Self-Improving Memory , a method for AI agents that manage their own memory. The model first discovers its own memory instructions. It then trains those skills into its weights. Co-authors include researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University. TL;DR Method: The base is Kimi-K2.6 , a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active and 256K context. Distillation adds a LoRA adapter (rank 64) on attention projections. Runs on: Training hardware is not disclosed. Kimi-K2.6 serving needs a multi-GPU node; Vast.ai recommends 8x H200 . Native INT4 weights exist. Performance: Self-found memory prompts average 56.0 on 3 tasks, versus 44.6 for the best human-written ones. Best: Codebase, 64.3 with optimized prompts, +20.6 over the best hand-written harness. Worst: Spectrum distillation adds only 2.9 points (46.5 vs 43.6 for SFT on generic runs). What is Self-Improving Memory? Self-Improving Memory is a 2-stage method from Meta FAIR that teaches an agent model to manage file-based memory. The agent works through a stream of subtasks. Each subtask starts with an empty context. Only a persistent memory directory, edited with file tools, carries over. Two prompts control that memory. OFFLOAD updates memory after a subtask. LOAD retrieves notes before the next one. Generic versions leave the strategy to the model. A pilot study in the research post found that no single hand-written strategy wins every task. How does harness optimization work? In stage 1, a meta agent rewrites the LOAD and OFFLOAD prompts. The search starts from 4 human-written seeds: Summary, Retrieval, Skill and Hypothesis. summary.tldr:
Meta FAIR, in collaboration with researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University, has introduced 'Self-Improving Memory,' a two-stage framework that enables AI agents to autonomously discover and distill optimal memory management strategies. The system utilizes the Kimi-K2.6 model—a 1-trillion parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with 32 billion active parameters and a 256K context window—to manage persistent file-based memory across subtask streams. By replacing static, human-written memory prompts with self-discovered instructions, the framework achieves an average score of 56.0 across three tasks, significantly outperforming the 44.6 average achieved by the best human-authored prompts.

The methodology operates in two stages: discovery and distillation. In the discovery phase, a meta-agent iteratively refines 'LOAD' and 'OFFLOAD' prompts by evaluating performance against a holdout set, evolving from four initial human-written seeds (Summary, Retrieval, Skill, and Hypothesis). The resulting prompts are highly specific, such as instructing the model to parse 'GUARDRAILS.md' and 'SCHEMA.md' before execution. In the second stage, these optimized strategies are distilled into the model weights using a LoRA adapter (rank 64) applied to attention projections. While the 'Codebase' task saw a substantial 20.6-point improvement over hand-written baselines, the 'Spectrum' distillation yielded more modest gains, improving from 43.6 to 46.5.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** The system is built on Kimi-K2.6, a 1T-parameter MoE model with 32B active parameters and 256K context, supporting native INT4 weights.
**Performance Metrics:** Self-discovered memory prompts achieved a 56.0 average score, compared to 44.6 for human-written prompts, with a peak performance of 64.3 in the Codebase task.
**Memory Mechanism:** Agents manage persistent file-based memory via two specific prompts: OFFLOAD (updating memory post-subtask) and LOAD (retrieving notes pre-subtask).

**Distillation Process:** The framework employs a 'Discover-Demonstrate-Distill' pipeline, utilizing LoRA adapters (rank 64) to bake optimized memory strategies directly into the model's attention projections.
**Hardware Requirements:** Kimi-K2.6 serving requires multi-GPU infrastructure, with recommendations suggesting an 8x H200 configuration.

title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
author: Dominic-Madori Davis
contentSnippet:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.

Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.

While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.

Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.

The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.

The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.

This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never

summary.tldr:
A recent wave of high-profile technical outages affecting major U.S. infrastructure—including the FAA, Microsoft (Outlook, Teams, Copilot), Apple Pay, and NASA—has sparked debate regarding the role of AI in systemic instability. While government officials and company spokespeople have largely attributed these incidents to non-malicious technical failures rather than state-sponsored cyberattacks, industry experts suggest these disruptions represent the 'growing pains' of integrating modern, AI-driven software with aging legacy infrastructure. The FAA outage, in particular, is cited as a case where modernization efforts overwhelmed legacy hardware incapable of handling modern data throughput.

Dave DeWalt, former CEO of McAfee and CISA Advisory Council member, argues that AI tools like Mythos are accelerating the discovery of long-standing vulnerabilities, forcing enterprises into a rapid, disruptive cycle of patching. Anusha Iyer, founder of the security startup Corsha, emphasizes that the core issue is not AI itself, but the rushed, poorly gated integration of modern systems into industrial environments that were never designed for such connectivity. Experts suggest that while these outages are causing significant short-term operational friction, they are also driving a shift toward more rigorous, AI-driven vulnerability management and autonomous remediation, creating a new market for resilience-focused security startups.
takeaways: **Infrastructure Impact:** Recent outages have disrupted critical systems including the FAA (grounding flights), Microsoft (Outlook, Teams, Copilot), Apple Pay, and NASA internal networks.
**Root Cause Analysis:** Experts attribute the instability to the rapid, un-gated integration of modern software with legacy hardware, rather than direct AI-driven cyberattacks.

**Vulnerability Discovery:** AI tools like Mythos are surfacing legacy security flaws at an unprecedented speed, forcing enterprises to perform emergency patching that causes secondary system disruptions.
**Market Opportunity:** Investors anticipate a surge in startups focused on AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, and secure infrastructure segmentation.

**Regulatory Context:** Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, has characterized these disruptions as a 'wake-up call' regarding the speed of AI adoption relative to management capabilities.

title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
author: Hazim Qudah
contentSnippet: Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it. Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in   SageMaker JupyterLab . Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings: Latency drift: A week-over-week rise in median (p50) end-to-end latency or time to first token. Unused capacity: GPUs you pay for that sit mostly idle. Configuration gaps: A serving container that’s missing newer performance improvements or security patches, or an optimization such as speculative decoding or GPU kernel tuning that your model supports but the endpoint doesn’t use. SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side

summary.tldr:
Amazon SageMaker AI has introduced a new Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature featuring an agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio, designed to detect latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on inference endpoints. The monitoring capability is enabled by default for all SageMaker AI inference endpoints utilizing vLLM serving containers and GPU instances without requiring manual setup, though users maintain the option to opt out.

The system analyzes operational signals such as latency, GPU utilization, and serving configurations without inspecting actual user requests or responses. From these signals, it generates three distinct categories of findings: latency drift (identifying week-over-week increases in median p50 end-to-end latency or time to first token), unused capacity (flagging GPUs that remain largely idle), and configuration gaps (spotting outdated serving containers missing recent security patches or performance improvements, as well as unutilized optimizations like speculative decoding and GPU kernel tuning).

When anomalies or optimization opportunities are detected, SageMaker AI dispatches notifications via AWS Health, consolidating findings per endpoint. These notifications link directly into the agentic experience within Amazon SageMaker Studio, prepopulating the endpoint and its recent traffic data so engineering teams can immediately execute inference recommendations to benchmark their current setup against alternative configurations.
takeaways: **Default Monitoring:** Automatically enabled for all SageMaker AI inference endpoints running on vLLM serving containers and GPU instances without requiring upfront user setup.
**Privacy-Preserving Telemetry:** Analyzes purely operational signals—specifically latency, GPU utilization, and serving configurations—without reading or logging user prompts and responses.

**Three Finding Types:** Detects week-over-week median (p50) latency/time-to-first-token drift, underutilized GPUs incurring unnecessary costs, and missing performance configurations like speculative decoding, kernel tuning, or container patches.

**Agentic Studio Integration:** Sends consolidated alerts through AWS Health that deep-link directly into an agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio pre-loaded with endpoint traffic data to benchmark alternatives.

title: Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews
author: Sunitha Srivatsa
contentSnippet: For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions?   Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring criteria to give candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Decades of research in industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology have shown that structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998; Sackett et al., 2022). Yet delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create q uestions, train interviewers, and evaluate responses consistently .   Amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups, and evidence-based scoring to help organizations gather consistent, job-related information while giving more candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their strengths. We built Connect Talent around three core design principles and evaluated how well the service applies them through a combination of internal research and independent expert review. The findings offer a closer look at the science behind Connect Talent’s AI-le d, structured interviewing.   Three core design principles 1. Build interviews around job-related evidence Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role. The service uses job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. Each scorecard defines specific strength and concern signals, and every interview question targets the behaviors it aims to uncover.   The AI interviewer also adapts to each response. After every answer, it checks whether the candidate has provided enough evidence for the competency being assessed. When details are missing, it asks targeted follow-up questions. This approach preserves the structure of the interview while giving candidates more opportunities to explain their experience.   2. title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() . title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor. Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday . He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.” Evasive and irregular turns “FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.” Read full article Comments

title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
author: Evandro Franco
contentSnippet: When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund. We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop. With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints. There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use. Strands capabilities, on AWS Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself. You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability. AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
author: Dave Salvator
contentSnippet: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . title: Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand
author: Suyin Wang
contentSnippet: Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
author: Ilan Geller
contentSnippet: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock , token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline. In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality. Attribution first: Measuring cost at the business level Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles , one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console , you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce. Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports , handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation count

title: From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League
author: Rakesh Vangari
contentSnippet: Cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again. AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
author: Mengxiao Wang
contentSnippet: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
author: Dmitry Soldatkin
contentSnippet: Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself. Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery. In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI . When one Region runs short of capacity A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it. How cross-Region inference routing works Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas: You decide where your model might run – For each model, you choose which endpoints and inference components the router might use. title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
author: Joe McCarron
contentSnippet: In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor . The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub. Agents act through tools, and tools move data Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back. That gap shows up in three ways: Sensitive data leaves through tool arguments. The model writes the arguments from everything in its context, including details the tool doesn’t need. Ask an agent about a customer, and the customer’s name, account number, or email goes straight into a query to a third-party server. That server sits outside your AWS account and your compliance scope. Sensitive data comes back in tool results. Scraped web pages, CRM records, and case notes land in the model’s context, memory, traces, and logs. This happens even when the task never needed them. Documents bypass text inspection. Document tools such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Box, and Google Drive return a signed URL, not text. A filter that inspects strings sees a link and lets it through, and the agent then opens the original file. Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool. AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor

title: 13 Best Agent Gateways in 2026 for MCP, A2A and LLM Traffic: Kong, Bifrost, AgentCore, Arcade
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Agents no longer just call a model. They call tools over MCP, delegate to other agents over A2A, and act inside business systems. An agent gateway is a control point that authenticates agents, filters the tools they see, and logs every call. A plain LLM gateway only routes model requests. title: Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Perplexity has launched the Perplexity Orchestrator API , a single endpoint for frontier and open-weight models. It picks a serving provider by availability, capacity and latency , and bills everything through 1 account. Developers get fewer integrations and 1 invoice. What is the Perplexity Orchestrator API? The Perplexity Orchestrator API is a hosted inference gateway that serves many models behind 1 base URL. It covers frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI . It also serves open-weight models such as GLM, Kimi and DeepSeek, hosted by Perplexity or inference partners. It accepts OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages requests. Most teams only change the API key and base URL. The OpenAI base URL is https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1 . Anthropic SDK users point at https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator , without /v1 . Perplexity runs the same layer internally, across 85+ models and more than a dozen providers. How does provider failover work? Failover keeps the model fixed and swaps the deployment. A Claude request that fails on Anthropic can be served by AWS Bedrock instead. The reliability docs set these rules: Triggers are provider errors, rate limits and timeouts. Each attempt has a time-to-first-token limit and a total-duration limit. The values are not published. Invalid or over-context requests return HTTP 400 and are not retried. If every deployment fails, the API returns HTTP 429 with Retry-After . Requests that fail before producing output are not billed. You cannot pick a deployment yourself. What do the reliability and speed numbers show? Perplexity measured production traffic from October 4 to November 2, 2026. Claude and GPT requests through Perplexity succeeded more often than requests to any single provider measured. Daily success rates also varied less during provider incidents. The post gives no percentage success rates. Speed varied by provider too. For Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic was fastest on 15 of 30 days, AWS Bedrock on 15. Azure’s median output speed for GPT-5.6 Sol was 27% higher than OpenAI’s. Speed-aware routing is still in progress. How does automatic routing with perplexity/auto work? Routing is in preview. PolyAI has released Dialog-RSN-1, a specialized reasoning model designed for real-time complex dialog, now available via AWS Marketplace and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. The model is engineered to process live audio input, reason about caller intent, and generate responses in a single pass, specifically targeting customer service automation. By deploying the model as a SageMaker endpoint, enterprises can integrate it directly into their existing AWS infrastructure, maintaining control over telephony, orchestration, and business logic while offloading the core audio-to-response reasoning task to PolyAI's architecture.

title: Former Alibaba exec’s Everful raises $48.5M to connect retailers with Chinese factories
author: Kate Park
contentSnippet:
Everful , a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.

The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.

Everful is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by the end of the year, about two and a half years after its launch, co-founder Sisi Song said. The company ships over 5 million items a month to customers in more than 60 countries and works with over 30,000 factory partners, she added. Its online wholesale catalog includes more than 20 million products.

Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous company to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.

Retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.

The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Big tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.

“We take care of everything,” Han said. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”

Everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song said, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everf

summary.tldr:
Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based B2B sourcing platform, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding. The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed. Founded in 2024 by former Alibaba executive Sisi Song and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, the company provides an end-to-end supply chain service that connects smaller retailers with over 30,000 Chinese factory partners. The platform currently manages over 20 million products in its wholesale catalog and is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue within roughly 30 months of operation.

Unlike traditional marketplaces that primarily facilitate transactions, Everful positions itself as a full-service provider that manages sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. The company utilizes AI agents to automate labor-intensive workflows, including trend tracking, supplier identification, and cross-factory coordination. Everful currently employs approximately 70 staff members, with 45 dedicated to R&D and AI operations. The company plans to use the new capital to expand its footprint in the U.S. and Europe—specifically the U.K., France, and Italy—and to further integrate its platform with e-commerce tools like Shopify to automate product customization.
takeaways: **Funding & Scale:** Raised $48.5 million in Series A; on track for $100 million in annualized revenue; ships over 5 million items monthly to 60+ countries.

**Operational Model:** Differentiates from competitors like Alibaba or Faire by taking full responsibility for the supply chain, including quality control and logistics, rather than acting solely as a transaction facilitator.
**AI Integration:** Employs AI agents to automate trend analysis, supplier matching, and logistics management, with a dedicated AI operations team bridging engineering and business functions.

**Geopolitical Strategy:** Actively managing U.S.-China trade risks, including potential shifts in the de minimis exemption, by focusing on a model of cross-border B2B sourcing paired with local retail sales.
**Expansion Plans:** Targeting growth in the U.S., U.K., France, and Italy, with a focus on deepening e-commerce platform integrations to serve as end-to-end infrastructure for global sourcing.

title: Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price
author: Russell Brandom
contentSnippet: Posted: 8:59 AM PST · November 19, 2026 Image Credits: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg / Getty Images Russell Brandom Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price Shares of Anthropic are now trading on the Nasdaq exchange, as the company successfully executes its initial public offering. In the early minutes of availability, shares were trading at $111.50, a 33% premium over the $83 IPO price. Set on Wednesday, the IPO price was already higher than the projected range set by the company, which anticipated a price between $70 and $78 per share. All told, the offering will raise over $81 billion, directed to a combination of employees and the company’s own coffers. The IPO funding, together with existing fundraising and new private offerings timed to coincide with the company’s public market debut, will leave Anthropic with an expected $220 billion in cash reserves. As one analyst told TechCrunch , “Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had.” The share price continues to fluctuate, but the opening price would put the company’s market cap over $2 trillion, making it more valuable than Meta, Tesla, or Walmart. Only five companies boast a higher valuation by market cap: Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft. In a speech before the opening bell , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized the company’s commitment to safety. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.” Newsletters See More Subscribe for the industry’s biggest tech news Related AI At Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO recommits to pacing AI development AI Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test Rebecca Bellan

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has officially debuted on the Nasdaq exchange, with shares opening at $111.50, representing a 33% premium over its $83 IPO price. The IPO price itself exceeded the company's initial projected range of $70 to $78 per share. The offering is set to raise over $81 billion, which will be distributed between employees and the company’s balance sheet.

Following the IPO and concurrent private offerings, Anthropic is projected to hold approximately $220 billion in cash reserves, a figure analysts suggest is unprecedented for a corporate entity. The opening share price places the company’s market capitalization above $2 trillion, positioning it as the sixth most valuable company globally, trailing only Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft, and surpassing Meta, Tesla, and Walmart.

CEO Dario Amodei utilized the opening bell ceremony to emphasize the company's "race to the top" philosophy, framing the IPO as a mechanism to secure the financial independence necessary to prioritize safety research. Amodei stated that the company aims to demonstrate that prioritizing safety does not preclude building a commercially successful enterprise.

**Market Valuation:** The opening price of $111.50 resulted in a market capitalization exceeding $2 trillion.
**Capital Reserves:** Anthropic expects to hold $220 billion in cash reserves following the IPO and associated private offerings.
**Market Standing:** The company is now the sixth most valuable by market cap, surpassing Meta, Tesla, and Walmart.
**Capital Raised:** The IPO is set to raise over $81 billion for the company and its employees.
